In the course of a lorg letter to the "Times," Mr. F Handel Booth, M.P., remarks : In spite of the tragedy of the whole business, one is forced to succumb to the temptation of extracting a little humour from the situation. That the guarantee fund will be a fiasco is obvious. My own estimate of the remuneration which the medical profession will receive In cash under the Act is five million pounds sterling. To say that those who are to receive this vast sum per annum will be financially ruined and needed protection of a few hundred thousand pounds is one of those things that no plain man of business can understand. Another smile will surely be pardoned to any one reading the declaration headed by a number of wealthy and titled doctors that they refuse to engage in attendance upon weekly wage-earners under the Act. It is much as if colliery directors and managers signed a pledge not to work at the coal face for a minimum sage. I have made inquiries in many districts, including the one I have the honour to represent, and have failed to discover any locality where the doctors will unitedly refuse to act on the panel. Still, it is just as well to point out what must be the inevitable result if in a given area the doctors refuse to serve, and the local committees are disinclined to make whole-time appointments at a fixed salary. The Act will not break down as the most ignorant suppose, but the medical benefit will be omitted and the insured person given the Zs. or Gs. 6d. allowed and asked to make his own arrangements. In the great bulk of cases he will be able to effect this by combination, and put a sum in his pocket which the Act has ear-marked for the doctor himself. Let us face the bedrock. Whilst in the West of Scotland at the recent by-elections I took considerable pains to examine the actual arrangements:of club practice. A large Glas- gow society contracts for its members, who are by no means the pick of the community, for the sum of 3s. per annum per head, including drugs and medicines. It SS well known that many Glasgow doctors are looking to the Insurance Act to considerably increase their incomes. Captain Campbell, the new Unionist M.P. for North Ayr, in the course of his campaign advertised a local mutual society; his contention was that better value was given in this particular town than could be given under the Act. The officers repudiated his account of their benefits, but that is by the way. The medical benefit, about which there was no controversy, is contracted for at the price of 2s. 6d. per head per annum, including drugs, ecc, and there is severe com- petition amongst doctors for the appointment. Apparently, if the wori ing men of Stewarton were given fis. 6d. and asked to make their own arrangements, they could do it, making a profit of Is. per man. Where would the medical profession gain anything by this alte:ation? Again in my own constituency 4s. per head is considered good market rate, and one society which arranges its prices per visit is able to do it for less. Strong pressure is consequently being brought upon me to have the amount allocated by the actuaries under the Act reduced.

Speaking of the jealousies, the over- lapping, and otherwise wasted energies, he pointed out the great responsibility, and indeed the necessity for union, and contended that- the first indispensable thereto is freedom from all outside control. Quoting Professor David Smith of Londonderry he said " Our land is vexed by sectarian animosity. The seamless robe of our blessed Lord is rent in fragments. And the cause is patent to every seeing eye. It is nothing else than the unholy alliance betweea Church and State, and there can never be peace in our land Until this is ended—until it is recognised that the State has no jurisdiction in the domain of conscience, and must cease from her long and persistent meddling." He spoke this way because in a very real sense the interests of every part of Christ's Church were as much to him es those of his own part. He was first and foremost a Churchman, he was coat a Free Churchman, and thirdly a Presbyterian Churchman. Speaking of the three great systems viz. : The Episcopalian, Presbyterian, and Independent, or the autocratic and democratic, with the representative system somewhere about midway between, of one or other of which all other systems were really a modification, be said that undoubtedly a sympathy existed between all churches even now. They might be unaware of it but it was there, and within a given area, all other things being reasonably near to normal, every part of the entire Church of Christ advinced or declined in very close sympathy with one another. Their people, and even more their ministers might be out of touch with one another, but the one Spirit withaut doubt pervaded to greater or lesser extent every church, and he believed that if we could rise to higher and worthier conceptions of her life the lower and dividing aspects would be completely submerged beneath an in-corning tide of God's spirit, leaving the highest and worthiest characteristics of each denomination as a ground for real union. He spoke of the proposed union in Canada of the Congregational, Methodist, and Presbyterian Churches into which the Anglican and Baptist corn- munions are not at present disposed to enter, quoting arguments in favour of organised unity, and against organised but in favour of unity in co-operation. Con- tending for organised unity he showed how Methodism with its circuits, districts, synods, &c., based on John Wesley's idea of a Presbyterian Church for England. Congregationalism with its coupling up movement of recent years, and Presbyterianism with its blend of Congregational independence, and representative goveinment, presented large grouni common to each upon which it ought not to be impossible to find enough standing room to unite organically, on the basis of a simple polity, the development of which along the lines agreed upon would be a matter of expediency dominated by outside circumstances. Speaking of the varied tastes in Church worship diets he said Presbyteri trism as at preeent was elastio enough to adopt a liturgy, which was actually done in some con- gregations, or to have the plainest service just as the people desired and decided, and still unite them all for active service. Speaking of creeds, he thought they I would all need to move in the direction of possessing a a simple creed, or of simplifying what they already possessed, simplicity in that as well as in Church polity being indispensable. The creed he would advocate would be something like this: "I believe in God, our Father. I believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer. I believe in the Infinite Spirit, the Revealer and Regenerator, and lastly and not least, I believe in a United Church." Speaking of the union of the United Presbyterian and the Free Churches of Scotland, and of the incalculable work performed by the late Principal Rainy, Mr. Reid referred to the sacrifice the Free Church was called upon to make by hhe decision of the House of Lords; how they manfully rose to it, and attempted not to retreat by an inch from the position taken up, and said that in every progressive work under- taken, sacrifice was invariably the price that had to be paid. The idea of Church Union to-day might be styled a visionary's dream, but he believed that within the next couple of decades the Church throughout the land would be compelled to this or some other solution of the problem we had with us to-day of increasing irreligion, and decline in Church life. Mr. William Walker and Mr. Hugh Hawthorne, jun., contributed to the discussion.

div.head: Rev. B. Percival on the Unrest of the Age.
div.p: Rev. B. Percival on the Unrest of the Age.

The Rev. B. Percival commenced his twentieth year as Vicar pf St. Peter's parish on Sunday. Preaching in the evening he took for his text the words—" The Lord thy God careth from the beginning of the year even unto the end of the year" Dent. xi. 12. He said the unrest which had teen manliest during the past year was not conficed to this country, nor to Europe; it was world-wide. There were constant upheavals, widespread political movements, industrial grievances and soei+l pralems of the highest magnitude, all Indicating national and individual unrest. Great states- men and wise counsellors had strenuously exercised their power to allay or mitigate this unrest, but with partial success, and to-day they had a well-known statesman appealing to the churches as the most potent and influential communities to deal with the matter. And he (the preacher) quite ogre( d with him. Th,) churches were in closer touth with the indivicb al. They might deal with the people politically in the masses but they could not do so in spiritual things. They must deal with the individual, and hence he was unable to understand why any man, or any bcdy of men, should at this time seriously propose to cripple the resources of the Church which had all too little nith which to carry on its organization could an one tell him how the severance of the Church in Wales from the Church of England was going to help in the matter ? Could anyone tell him what spiritual good was going to be done to any person, or how the Kingdom of Christ Vitlls to be extended by taking 18s. 61. in the £ from the Church in Wales ? He appealed to all parties to consider this question most carefully and earnestly. Would it not be better to contribute to the Church's resources so that she might be able to employ more godly men and women to go among the MaSSES, speak to them individually, take them by the hand, and convince them that they cared for them, and that God cared for them all and each ? His experience was that from the moment they got a man to realise what he had said, rest came to him, and his condition and environment began to improve.

The " British Congregationalist" publishes some very interesting New Year messages from leaders of the denomination. Mr. Gerard Ford, the honoured chairman of the Union, reminds us that 1912 will be a time of retrospect. "It is well," he says "for us to be reminded that the call to be Nonconformists is as imperative as it was 250 years ago, and that the State is as insistent on its authority over the Church as it was when the Confessors or 1662 gave up their livings to save their souls." Principal Forsyth's message is also most irspiring. Why does be not always speak in this straight, simple language ? " Never mind the numbers in our churches," he writes, "keep up their hearts, increase their faith. The Lord is nearer His church than ever. . . Was it not something of the joy of the Lord that found us when we read Mr. Lloyd George's speech last week? The church less of a party, and more of a power; less of an irritant, more of an inspiration; more of a conscience whose judgment begins at the house of God; rrore of an 'apostle, more of a sacrificial deliverer for society! ' Other cheering messages are from Principals Selbie and Garvie, Dr. Bevan, Dr. Goodrich, and the Rev. Arnold Thomas. The " Congregationalist" begins the sear well.

Lord Haldane and Co-operation in
Defence.

Viscount Haldane, Secretary for War, speaking at Edinburgh on Monday night, said that while Lord Roberts was perhaps the greatest living commander of troops, he disagreed with him as to defence, but he welcomed Lord Roberts's more generous attitude to the Territorial Force. "I am a politician of some quarter of a century's experience," said Lord Haldane," and speaking as something of an expert, I venture to predict that no political party will take up compulsory national service in this country as a practical question in your lifetime or in mine." In conclusion, Lord Haldane referred to the new Naval War Staff. " Like the Army," he said, " the Navy has now got a general staff. That means that the Navy and the Army are going to co-operate in the problem of defence in a fashion we have never done before. Theso two staffs have above them a great general staff in the Defence Committee. We have now got as fine an organization as there is in the world." (Cheers).

div.head: OUR PREPAREDNESS FOR WAR.
div.p: OUR PREPAREDNESS FOR WAR.
Lord Haldane and the National Reserve.

Viscount llaldane, Secretary for War, on Tuesday fulfilled a number of engagements at Glasgow. Speak- ing at a representative meeting of Glasgow citizens in the City Chamber on the subject of the National Reserve, he said his studies had led him to believe that until the world was a little better than it was at the present time the surest way to prevent war was to be ready in case we were attacked.(Hear, hear.) He did not believe anybody wished to attack us at this mom.nt, and he was sure we did not wish to attack anybody. But we must be in a position to take care of ourselves, He bad been at the War Office longer than any predecessor for a long time, and with the advice of the distinguished generals trained by the lessons of South Africa, and with much assistance derived from study at close hand of German organisa- tion, ideas began slowly to form themselves. Ile had been privileged to go to Berlin as the guest of the Emperor, there to study the German army system, and out of the incoherent forces which existed after the South African War he and his staff had organised the Expeditionary Army which could now be mobilised in ten days. It was a small army, but was better trained than a Continental army, and it was designed for the special sevices which it might be called on to perform abroad or at home. Then there was the Territorial Force, organised on the same pattern as the Regulars. The secret of vitality of an army was its close contact with national life. Thus there were the Boy Scouts, the Cadet organisation, and the Officers' Training Corps, which, while peaceful formations' yet incul- cated that training and discipline which made them admirable recruiting grcunds for the Territorial and Regular forces. A CORCE HITHERTO UNTOUCHED . _ • . . .

But beyond that there had remained a force which bad not been touched till the other day, the National Reserve. Young men joining the army at eighteen, after completing their seven years' service and five years in the Ftesorves, were still only thirty years of age. They and others older had still a lot of fighting in them. Here was a mAgnificent force of strength hitherto untouched. It was of these men that the National Reserve could he formed, and their first idea was to get a complete register of all the men who had served with the colours in the Regular Army, the old Volunteers, the Territorials, and the Navy, so that if a national emergenoy arrived appeals could be made to these trained and disciplined men to return to the flag. Even the oldest veterans could do something, if only in the way of encouraging younger men. Lord Roberts had corns forward as chief of the National Reserve, and Lord Haldane appealed to ex-service men in Glasgow at least to register themselves in the roll of the nation's trained men.

The Board of Trade Returns for 1911 just published establish a fresh record for British Commerce. The aggregate reached for the year is £1,238,000,000. Mr. Chamberlain declared that the great edifice of British trade was in imminent danger of collapsing like the Campanile of Venice and burying British power and prestige in its ruins. It is singular how such an astute man was deceived by the depreciation in values. Why Mr. Chamberlain allowed himself to go so far astray has been a mystery to everyone. We can only account for it that his desire to consolidate the Empire got such an over mastering hold upon his mind, time, and energy, that it left no room for even a superficial study of the economic problem upon which his crude plan depended. The course of his campaign as far as it related to economics was thickly strewn with the wreckage of what he thought to be true facts and inferences, whilst every prophecy he made in relation to the future of British industry under Free Trade has been falsified. The diagram we here reproduce illustrates one important fact the oversight of which misled Mr. Chamberlain. The black line

indicates the growth according to actua• values, the dotted line the growth, supposing the goods had continued at the same values as at the year 1872 from which his calcula- tions started. It will be seen from our diagram that the real progress in the commerce of the country has been continuous and fairly regular, but that since 1892 the growth has been more rapid. Mr. Chamberlain in one of his fiscal speeches in 1903 said "It is to our exports, I will not say entirely—but mainly— that we must look for the test of the progress of our trade." Taking the exports alone by value the difference between 1872 and 1902 was as Mr. Chamberlain pointed out, an increase of 28 millions only. But since the year he spoke the increase has been 171 millions. The slow growth both in the export and the total trade between 1872 and 1902 was only apparent and the growth between 1902 and 1911 has to be discounted by a rise in values, but this rise is not nearly equal to the drop between 1872 and 1902. As soon as the 1911 figures for the principal competing countries are to hand, we propose by diagram to show the relative growth.

Balfour was anxious about market gardeners, Lord Rothschild was worried over industrial workers,and Mr. Austen Chamberlain posed as the champion of small holders. But" number one " was really the individual whom the opponents of the Budget were most think- ing about. (Hear, hoar.) The bitter cry of ruined aristocrats who represented the land taxes as the end of all things " was sheer bunkum. The Lords threw out the Budget and then ensued the great tattle for the people's rights. The triple or " tipple " alliance a hich Mr. Balour had at his command—Lords, Land and Liquor—did their best and worst. But the political trumpet blew with no uncertain sound, the result being a pronounced and unmistakable majority against the Peers and for the Liberal Budget. (Applause). Hitherto it could not be honestly said that the Liberals had had a fair chance with their proposed legislation. It had always been a case of loaded dice. The people having at two succes- sive elections given their verdict in clear and emphatic terms, the Government lost no time in coming to close grips a ich the Lords. Lord Lansdowne ingeniously attempted to draw the teeth of democracy, but such an occupation should certainly be scheduled in the "dangerous " section. (Laughter.) Someone's teeth had to be drawn, but it was not those of the democracy lion. Reference hiving been made to the tactics of the " Die Herds " and the " Hughligans," the lecture touched upon the great work of Mr. Asquith in piloting the Parliament Bill. His courage, straightness and devotion to the people's cause filled, every Liberal's heart with pride and joy that he was their leader. He took his place with the great heroes of Liberalism. (Applause.) Was it fully realized what the victory won for the people meant ? Seventy nine, years ago the great Reform Bill was passed. Ever since that time the hateful fetters of the hereditary legislature had always been on the limbs of the electors. On August 10th, 1911, those fetters were struck off and democracy stood triumphant. (Applause) But they must remember that they had yet to reap the harvest. There were great arrears of legislation to fetch up and they must not expect to see every reform which was dear to their hearts placed upon the Statute BOA in one year or two. Finally the lecturer called attention to the nobler battle in which Mr. Lloyd George had been eagaged. In the cartoon now shown he was depicted as a wood- man grappling with ugly briars and undergrowth, such as consumption, sickness, disease and unemployment. The Insurance Act was truly one which "strikes the imagination of the world." It was the most far-reaching project of social legislation ever yet laid before an country in the world. (Applause). Much was being made of the fourpence a week payment, but when they considered the five benefits—medical, sanatorium, sickness, disablement and maternity—it must be admitted that those were priceless boons. The Act meant that never again would there be a heavy account to settle for medical attend- ance when the breadwinner was down, and the sick pay would just keep the family's head ab3va water at the critical time. It made a new era of legislation and they might well be proud of belonging to the party responsible for placing the measure upon the statute book. (Applause).

div.head: "SIX YEARS OF LIBERAL GOVERNMENT."
div.p: "SIX YEARS OF LIBERAL GOVERNMENT."
Lectures at the Liberal Club.

An interesting series of lantern lectures on " Six years of Liberal Government" has been given at the Liberal Club during the past week, before the workers of the various wards. The lectures accompany a series of F. C. Ge's inimitable cartoons from the "Westminster Gazette" and present political truths in a bright and attractive style. Monday evening wr,s sot apart for St. John's Ward and, despite the unfavourable weather,there was a good attendance. Mr. Hinny NEW delivered the lecture which empha. sised the clear line of demarcation between the two great parties in the State ; and contrasted the fruits of six years of Liberal Government with the poor results of ten years of Tory rule. Reference was made to the efforts of the Liberal administration to remedy the great injustice of Mr. Balfour's Education Act of 1902 and to the wrecking tactics which the Lords pursued. But the end was not yet. Before long another attempt would be made, tbla time with much greater chance of success. Mr. Asquith had written that " We cannot allow the present injustices and the limitations or absence of popular control, to continue to deface our educational system." With regard to industrial questions, previous to the 1900 election much was heard in workingclass centres of the Tariff Vale decision. For thirty-years every one thought Parliament intended by the 1871 Act to legalise trade unions. In 1901 the House of Lords decided otherwise. No attempt was made by the Tory Government to remove the difficulties thus created. The Liberals supported the right of effective combitiatiop and by the Trades Disputes Act succeeded in making it secure. The measure passed the House of Lords. although Lord Halsbury denounced it as "disgraceful, "tyrannicarand "outrageously unjust." Lord Lansdowne said " They were passing through a period when it was necessary for the House of Lords to move with groat caution. Let their lordships, so far as they were able, be sure that if they were to join issue, they did so upon ground which was as favourable as possible to them- selves. In this case the ground would be unfavourable." The only assumption to be drawn from this was that the Lords were afraid of organised working- men. (Applause.) On the question of national defence,the lecturer pointed out that Lord Haldane was pre-eminently a strong man with ideas, and the War Office had afforded a fine field for the display of his talents. He had faced the question of re-organisation boldly and bed honestly aimed at efficiency and economy. As a fighting machine (although they hoped it might be many a day before it was required) our Army was more fit than for years past. (Applause.) The Tories had carried on a shameful campaign against the Liberal Government on the subject of the navy. The country rang with charges which, had they been true, should have brought every admiral in Whitehall to the scaffold. (Laughter). The real fact was, of course, that Liberals realised quite as well as any Tory that our Navy must be strong. But Liberals were not willing recklessly to squander the nation's money to oblige panic-mongering Tories, who called everyone a traitor who mai not prepared to join them in folly. The Navy estimates for 1911-12 were £41,39'2,100—an increase of £3,178.000 en 1910-11. A praise Northy.attempt was mate by the Goverment to effect some improvement in licensing matters. That reform was really of a very moderate character, but the wildest and moat absurd sta'ementi sera made about robbing widows and orphans whose money was invested in breweries. The Bill, having taken six weeks of Parliamentary time, passed the House of Commons, and In two hours at an impertinent meeting of Tory Peers at Lansdowne House it was slaughtered. The loss of the Bill was to be regretted, especially because it would have given back to the State the control over licences which it ought never to have abandoned. But Mr. Balfour gave the word that it must be rejected, and the Lords obeyed. After all their many promises to give old age pensions, the Tories refused to vote for pensions although they were afraid to vote against them. On the third reading 11 Tories voted against the Bill, 12 voted for it, and 110 did net vote at all. At the Trade Union Congress at Ipswich, Mr. D. J. Shackleton, then Labour M.P., speaking as president, said: "No Act of Parliament has given greater satisfaction, brightened more homes, and gladdened more hearts than this.' (Applause.) Reference was next made to the fical question, the fact being emphasised that Liberalism stands between the people and Protection. Warrington's Misfortunes. Saturday was indeed an unfortunate day for Warring- ton. The fixture was with Huddersfield, the cleverest and best drawing team in the Union, whose visit had been eagerly looked forward to by the Wirepullers' supporters. A record crowd would have been assured but for the weather,which was of the vilest description. Rain had fallen for twenty-four hours, and on Saturday was mingled with storms of sleet. The ground was in a shocking state, under water in places, and not fit for serious football. Warrington were strongly averse t playing, but Huddersfiald persisted, and eventually the Referee decided that the match must proceed. The gates were then opened and about 1,500 people swarmed on to the stands. The home team was disorganised by the absence of Brooks, Bradshaw, and Woodburn, while the visitors were well-represented. War- rington had the advantage of the wind, and rushed the ball through the mud in energetic style, a lofty punt causing a° visitors some anxiety. Holland cleared strongly, but a dashing dribble by Renwick and Way- well forced the ball over, and Wagstaffa was lucky to race up and save. Huddersfield now took up the running and strong play by Wrigley and Wagstaffe forced Warrington to defend. Turning round, Wagstaffe and Wildman placed the Yorkshiremen in a good position. The visiting forwards were early aggressive, Clark leading them fiaely to the line, where Renwick was decidedly lucky in holding up Wildman. For a long time the game became almost farcical. Wagstaffa saved repeatedly by forcing the ball out of play, and eventually he was the means of the Tykes adding to their score, for dribbling accurately, the home three-q rafters made ineffectual attempts to check and Kitchen crossed at the corner. Wrigley again failed. The game was keenly fought out until the close and in the end the visitors retired winners. Result : Hudderzfield, two tries (six points) ; Warrington, nil.

There was only a light agenda for discussion at the monthly meeting of the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday evening and the proceedings were concluded in about half-al.-hour. The Mayor (Councillor Dr. Joseph) presided and there were also present :—The Deputy-Mayor (Alderman Forshaw), Aldermen A Bennett, T Burton, John Evans, James Evans, J Smethurst and D Tinnion, Councillors G Archer, T H Ashcroft, W II BeLink, T Birtles, T Chantler, J G Craik, E Cunnington, J Dickenson, J Halliwell, J Hawthorn, It Henshall, C Jackson Holmes, W H J Jenkins, F T Lashford, J Pemberton, II Roberts, .1 Sankey, T S Steel, 0 Toole, J Wilkinson and W J Wilson, Messrs J L Whittle (town clerk), A T Hanewsy (deputy town clerk), T H Spinks (assistant town clerk), .1 Fairhurst (borough treasurer), W S Haddock (gas engineer), F V L Mathias (electrical engine r), J M Murray (director of education). STREEr IMPROVEMENT.

The Town Clerk, at a Meeting of the Finance am! Estate Committee, presented the sanction of the Local Government Board to the borrowing of the sum of £21,992 for the purposes of street improvement. SITE FOR A NEW SCHOOL.

At a meeting of the Finance and Estate Committee, the Town Clerk laid before the members the sanction of the Local Government Board to the borrowing of the sum of £1,271 for the purchase of land in Oakwood- avenue and Steel-street as a site for a public elementary school. On the motion of Councillor WILKINSON, seconded by Alderman .SMETII CRST, the minutes of thesommittee were carried. ASSISTANT INSPEC TOR OF NUISANCES APPOINTED.

A meeting of the Health Committee was held on December 10th, when the six candidates selected to appear before this committee for the appointment of assistant inspector of nuisances, having been inter- viewed, it was resolved, that James Monks, of Warrington, be appointed at a salary of £7B per annum and uniforin, rising by annual increments (on satis- factory service), of .£6 lOs to a maximum of £125. "UNFIT FOR THE FOOD OF MAN."

On the minutes of the Health Committee, Councillor CHINTLER called attentioa to the follow- ing :—" The Town Clerk reported that, in accordance with the instructions of the committee, proceedings had been taken against the person in whose possession the carcase of a sheep, which was unfit for the food of man, had been found, and that a penalty of 20s. and costs had been inflicted." From whom, he asked, was the sheep received ? Alderman JAMES EVANS : We know where it came frbm and all the circumstances surrounding the case, but the only person we have to deal with is the person in whose possession the carcase was found. The minutes were approved. TOUTING IN THE CEMETERY. At a meeting of the Cemetery Committee the Registrar reported upon the growing practice of canvassing in the cemetery for orders for the turfing of graves and the supply of memorial stones, &c., and it was resolved that the Town Clerk be r«riested to have notices printed and posted et the ,Cemetery, intimating that touting is strictly prohibited, and that a letter to the same effect be seat to the persons con- cerned and that all persons having work to execute in the Cemetery be first required to produce to the Registrar an authority signed by the owner of the grave. The Registrar was directed to discontinue the practice of publishing, for the information of stone- masons and others,a list of interments at the Cemetery. The minutes were approved. MUNICIPAL BOWLING GREENS.

POSITION OF NEW PAVILION CRITICISED. At a meeting of the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee, the Borough Surveyor submitted a plan for the construction of a bowling green and pavilion at Grace's Pottery, at an estimated cost of £755 and it was resolved that the same he approved, and that the Town Clerk be instructed to apply to the Local Govern- ment Board for their sanction to the borrowing of the sum of £755. Alderman SMETHURST moved and Councillor HALL-I-WELL seconded, the passing of the minutes. Alderman BENNETT said he hoped proper care would be taken to see that the pavilion was put in the right position at Grace's Pottery. He made that remark in view of the absolutely foolish way in which the matter had been mismanaged in St. Elphin's Park. He had nothing to sty particularly about the pavilion itself, but it was in such a position as to obscure the view of the College. The back of the structure was visible to everyone riding in the tram, for at least a quarter of a mile, the end laced the road, and the opportunity had been missed of making the pavilion tit in harmoniously with the whole of the surroundings. In its present position the pavilion, instead of being an ornament, was an eyesore. (Hear, hear.) It seemed to hit people in the face and give them a pain in the eyes every time they saw it. (Laughter). Councillor JENKINS said Aldermaa Bennett forgot that in erecting a pavilion the comfort and protection of the bowlers was the primary object, and not merely what other people liked. Alderman BENNETT : Not the sole object, surely. Councillor CRAIK said he did not know about the primary object, but be failed to see why only common bricks should have been put in the side of the building that faced Manchester-road and Ruabon bricks at the back. Councillor PEMBERTON : The Corporation generally do that kind of thing—do things wrong way about. Alderman BENNETT: They always do. Councillor PEMBERTON : It is perfectly ridiculous to build a pavilion in that position. some regard ought to have been paid to the appearance of the thing from the high road. The position of the pavilion would not be material to the comfort of the bowlers. Councillor WILKINSON : All this is out of order. There is no reference to St.Elphin's park in the minutes. Alderman BENNETT : It is simply brought forward as an illustration to prevent similar mistakes in the future. Councillor WILKINSON said that to ease Alderman Bennett's mind, he would see that the green and pavilion at Grace's pottery were put in the right place. Tbere was nothing they could obscure there. (Laughter). Councillor HAWTHORN: I hope that not only will the green at Grace's pottery be put in the right place, but that we shall have one in Wbitecross Ward. Alderman JAMES EVANS I And all over the town (Laughter) The minutes were agreed to. GAS COOKERS AS CUPBOARDS.

Aldermen JOHN EVANs moved and Councillor WILKINSON seconded, the confirmation of the minutes of the Gas Committee. Councillor PEMBERTON asked when the committee intended to meet the demand for slot meters and gas stoves ? It was unfair to poor gas consumers not to do so. He did not wish to do anything contrary to the wish of the committee, but if they were not prepared to act on his suggestipn he should bring forward a special resolution asking the Corporation to take the matter up. The Corporation had the monopoly of the gas and some buainess method ought to be adopted. They should not play with the consumers as they were doing at present. Alderman JOHN EVANS, in reply, said the reason the supply of slot meters for cooking purposes had been withheld was that the committee had found that a large proportion of the meters had not been used. The Ovens were used more as cupboards than anything else. (Laughter). In many cases the fixing of the ovens and meters cost the committee about 30s. each, and there had not been a pennyworth of gas going through them. It was therefore necessary to curtail the supply of slot meters. Councillor PEmBERTos : It is penalising the people who want to use them. .
Alderman JOHN EVANS They can get them, but they will have to pay for the fixing. The minutes were passed. TEIE WATER SUPPLY.

div.head: UNION OF CLERKS.
div.p: UNION OF CLERKS.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Branch of the National Union of Clerks was held at the Labour Exchange on Tuesday. The chief business was a retrospect of the goad work done by the Union during the past 12 months. The following were the principal features :—Two thousand eight hundred new members enrolled. Minimum wage. The West Ham Borough Council has adopted this: The Rhondda U.D.C. also accepted a re-organisation scheme on our normal minimum as a basis. In connection with the latter it is the interesting fact that after a thorough inquiry as to the merits of the N.U.C. and the two sectional Municipal Associations, the staff decided in favour of the Union and to-day all those eligible are members of the N.U.C. Inspection of offices. This has advanced a stage. Our offspring,the Offices Regulations Bill, was introduced by Mr. C. %V. Bowerman in the House of Commons, but did not get beyond the first reading, owiag to the demands made by the Government upon the time of the legislators. The Bill will be re-introduced this year, and it is hoped it will make better progress in view of the many promises of support given us by 'AP's. The Port of London Authority Clerks at one time had a email Association of their own that sent up petition after petition to the authority but these were ignored, and in August they decided to join the N.U.C. The Union set to work and sent in a petition to head- quarters, and on December let the clerks received the first instalment of the N.U.C.'s demands which is estimated to amount to £ll,OOO per annum. At the beginning of September, 1910, One of our Birmingham members was given notic3 b y a Brewery Company on the grounds of cutting down expenses owing to "a thing called the Budget." At the time he had a first class reference given to him. He found out afterwards the reason given for his dismissal was not correct, as his work was being done by his predecessor and a Corporat'on clerk who WAS putting in his evenings to do • book-keeping. The member wrote to the " Birmingham Daily M nil " about this, and the cap evidently fitted the manager and another Corporation clerk, also putting in evening work for the Company, both of whom wrote letters strongly condemning" Live and let live." Later on the member had an offer of a per- manent position provided a testimonial, obtained direct from the firm, was equal to the one he was carrying about with him in his pocket. The Manager of the Brewery instead of repeating his former testimonial, wrote as follows :—" Our short experience of Mr. Blocksedge has been most unpleasant and unsatisfac- tory, and we Prefer to say nothing more about the man." It will be seen that a character of this nature was sufficient to damn any man for life, and fortunately fell into our hands. Not getting satisfaction from the company the matter was placed in the hands of Mr. Danes, a Birmingham solicitor. On his and counsel's advice the Executive decided to issue a writ for libel, the case was heard on December 4th and .sth. We were represented by Mr. E Cave who handled our position very skilfully. The jury eventually brought Ins verdict for the plaintiff with £2O damages and costs, his character at the same time being publicly retrieved. An instance like this shows how necessary it is that the Character Vote Bill should be pressed forward as speedily as possible, so as to compel employers to hand to their employee 3 on leaving their service a written character, so that it may be known exactly what as said about them, and to prevent employres giving "characters " over the telephone, or in some other secret manner, detrimental to the interest of the worker In November three new Branches were formed, St. Helens, Stoke-on-Trent, and Surrey Commercial D.E.

If Sir EDWARD CARSON is victorious in the House of Commons there will be no occasion for him to be triumphant in the field. From Sir EDWARD CARSON, however, there comes no glorious anticipation of the rout of Wome Rule. He seems, on the contrary, to be anticipating disaster for himself. He is a Privy Coun - cillor, he tells us, and he does not care 'one farthing about forfeiting this, or any other honour which has been conferred on him

According to Sir EDWARD CARSON,nothing has changed in regard to the Home Rule question since 1893. To other observers it must appear that almost everything has changed. A little more than a year ago there Were perfervid Conservative newspapers Which were advocating Home Rule and even Home Rule all round, as a means of bringing the Conservative Party back to power; and the old familiar attitude was only resumed in face of a General Election, in which the despairing cry of " Let us bid farewell to reason" was the prelude to the rising of the time-honoured war whoop. We do not remember that anything of this kind Preceded the introduction of the H ome Rule -Bill of 1893. Then, too, there was some measure of sincere argument. Men were not being drilled into rebellion as a means of intimidating the House of Commons. It is a , cause already lost which resorts to such methods, either of oratory or of organisation, as those of Sir EDWARD CARSON. Colonel Edward Herbert THE LATE COLONEL Fitzherbert, whose FITZHERBERT. death is recorded this week, is affectionately remembered by many Warringtonians for the keen interest which he took in the welfare of "Private Tommy Atkins." It was entirely due to his initiative and energy that the Soldiers' Club in Bewsey-road was established. One of the chief objects was to provide a memorial of the South African campaign and at the same time to cater for the wholesome recreation of the soldiers stationed in Warrington. Admiable club premises were found in the house •formerly occupied by Mr. Ziba Armitage and subsequently Mr. H. Milling, Mr. T. Pilkington and Dr. Adams. The build- ing was in every way adapted for the purpose, being large, lofty, well-lighted and airy. It was carefully re-papered and painted, and the walls hung with pictures,. There was a game room, with billiard table, chess and draughts, a well stocked library, committee-room, bathrooms, bedrooms, a reception room for sergeants and their friends. Coffee and light refreshments could be obtained, but no intoxicants were sold. The club was opened on July 2nd, 1902, by Major-General Hallam Parr, C. 8., of Chester, and in the course of a speech at the ceremony Colonel Fitzherbert said the establishment of the club redeemed the pledge which he gave to the Active Service Company on its departure for South Africa. For a time the club was greatly appreciated and did well, but somehow interest gradually languished and the institution ceased to exist about four years ago.

Free Traders have THE OVERSEAS never maintained that TRADE. our overseas trade was an infallible criterion of prosperity, or that Free Trade, under all and every conditions, was certain to produce prosperity. But the whole case for Tariff Reform from the very first lay over the corpses of dead and dying industries, Mr. I Chamberlain, in launching his revolutionary I propaganda, recognised that the burden of proof rested upon his economic heresy. His case was that the trade of this country ought to be measured by its exports, and that the export trade, owing to F ree Trade policy, I had been stationary for thirty years. I If we take Mr. Chamberlain's test, and to take it is to allow Tariff Reform to choose its own ground, we find that the Tariff Reform case is entirely refuted by facts. Mr. Chamberlain pitched on a thirty years' period as "a fair time to go back." He elected to submit the prosperity of this country, under Free Trade, to the test of progress, or failure to progress, during that period. Well, during the last thirty years, British exports have increased by ninety-two per cent. When Tariff Reform has chosed its own ground so deliberately, and so emphatically been con- victed of error, there is nothing more to be said.

We understand that TEMPERANCE.WORK the United Kingdom IN WARRINGTON. Alliance has appointed Mr. Thomas D. Leslie, of Wigan, to work for the cause of Temper- ance in Warrington for half his time, the other half being given to Wigan, where he resides. The temperance party in our Borough has long lacked the cohesion necessary to make its efforts effective. It is now proposed to makethe Warrington Citizen's Temperance League a central organization, and the differ- ent Temperance Societies are to be asked to send a representative to act on a united executive. We are glad to know this League is not confined to abstainers, but welcomes the help of all who desire so to con- trol the facilities for drinking, that they, may be limited to legitimate needs, reduced where unnecessary, and not forced upon new localities against the wishes of large majorities. We desire to impress upon our Temperance friends, in their efforts to strengthen and make effective public control, the necessity of securing the co-operation of the moderate citizen. It'is only by so doing they can exptfct to carry reforms in connection with public administration, to regulate the number and character of licensed houses, and return to the Council men independent of the influence and control of the Trade. In such matters as the effect of the consumption of alcohol uPon the body, the economic waste caused by the large expenditure, the public burden in dealing with the fruits of the traffic, all these give ample scope for public advocacy and moral suasion. But when you come to such ques- tions as public control it is well to acknow- ledge that it is folly to race ahead of the growth of public opinion, and it is equal folly to try to effect moderate reform without the co-operation of moderate men. There are many who believe that alcohol in moderation is a very innocent sort of poison, but at the same time realise clearly all the evils direct and indirect of its con- sumption in excess, and therefore are pre- pared to go far with the Temperance people in supporting further restrictions of the superfluouS facilities for drinking in the Borough. Such also can unite in returning to the Town Council only those who are beyond suspicion of having any axe to grind. In these matters all reformers should unite, and go forward together. A new and brighter era in local Temperance work is lover-due.
In December, the "SEE HIM BOILED Australian Customs FIRST." brought into operation
a revised tariff on certain imports, including the following British goods:

Leather cloth, formerly flee: now dutiable at 20 per cent. Electric and gas appliances, stoves, Tendants. brackets, &c.: duty increased from 20 per cent. to 25 per cent. Gas meters, formerly free: now dutiable at 15 per cent. Gramophones, &3., formerly free: now dutiable at 30 per cent. Motor Chass's, formerly free: now dutiable at 10 per cent. In spite of the fact that on the above-men- tioned articles the duties applying to Great Britain have been raised, we shall still have our Protectionists here quoting Australia as having given special preferential treatment to us without a corresponding return on the part of Great Britain, and calling Free Traders all kinds of names for rejecting "offers," and what not. Well, the latest " offer " from Australia is to make it harder for British manufacturers to trade with her in leather goods, stoves, gramophones, etc. It is true that we are subjected to a tariff slightly lower than that which applies to foreign nations. But why should this lead British Protectionists to reproach the Government for its "unsympathetic atti- tude" towards the Colonies? The benefit which British manufacturers receive through

this visionary preference is inconsiderable. Australia has set up, as Protectionists at home urge us to set up here, a tariff against all other competing nations, in order that the Australian manufacturers may exploit unchallenged the customers in their home market. Their object is to secure the posi- tion of their own Australian manufacturers against both British and foreign competitors. And the slightly differential treatment between British and foreign goods is pointed to as a sacrifice made by the Colony in favour of Great Britain. In face lof the great handicap under which British goods have to compete in Australia with home manufactures we are unable to see the "sacrifice,:' or the need for a " return" on the part of the Mother Conntry. The fact is that no amount of Imperial pleading will stay our Colonists from exercising their industrial genius in their own way. Are they not the offspring of an industrial race? And we have ample evidence that it is their intention to develop their industries to the fullest possible extent. It is sufficient to give one Australian reply to Mr. Chamber- lain's famous appeal. Said Mr. Chamber- lain, at Glasgow, on October 6th, 1903 : " There are many things which you (the Caonies) do not make now, many things for which we have a great capacity of production. Leave them to us as you have left them hitherto." And the repl3 of the "Sydney Bulletin" was as a final as it was crude :
" We will see Mr. Chamberlain boiled first."

A leaflet distributed at one of the anti- Home Rule meetings addressed by Sir Edward Carson displays the disloyalty of these frenzied factionists to an amazing degree. The leaflet claims justification for asking " the greatest Protestant nation on earth, Germany, to come over and help us once again to break the power of Rome in Ireland." A similar proclamation in Germany itself would result in the rebels being promptly put in prison. Here we'rely on the national sanity to relegate people of this class to their proper place.

There seems to be a variety of opinions among farmers and horse-owners about the wisdom of tar-spraying the main roads, but there will be none among the ordinary road- users. The tar-sprayed roads which have come under our notice have been wonderfully clean and free from dust in the dryest •weather, while their capacity for hard wear has also been manifest even to the untrained eye. We are glad to note that the Lancashire County Council has been promised a grant of £5,000 for the next two years by the Roads Board, and hope that the tar- spraying will be widely exten3ed. * * *

Three deans of English cathedrals have recently attained their 80th birthday. Dr. Darby, Dean of Chester, attained that age on November 20th; Dr. Fremantle, Dean of Ripon, on December 12th; and Dr. Pigou, Dean of Bristol, on Monday, January Bth. The Dean of Llandaff is 86, the Dean of Durham 84,. and the Dean of Exeter 84, so that there are six octogenarian occupants of decanal stalls, but not one of an Episcopal throne, the oldest bishop being Dr. Forrest Browne, Bishop of Bristol, who recently con- templated retirement, but has been persuaded "in an authoritative quarter "(probably Lambeth) to remain at his post. *

Paisley Abbey, towards the restoration of which a sum of .00,000 has been given, dates from the 12th century. It belonged to the Cluniacensians, and is memorable as the burial place of the ancestors of the Stuart family. It was suppressed in 1559, amid scenes of the wildest fanaticism. " They fumigated the church with burnt wool and feathers instead of incense," writes Sir Walter Scott, "put foul water into the holy water basins; they sang ludicrous and indecent parodies to the tunes of church hymns; they violated whatever vestments belonging to the abbey they could lay their hands upon; and played every freak which the whim of the moment could suggest to their wild caprice." * * *

In at least one Lancashire district there has lately been an alarming growth of the half-time evil. In two schools during the last few weeks there have been fourfold and fivefold increases in the numbers of children applying for exemption certificates as com- pared with the figures of former years. Inquiry among the parents (says the " Man- chester Guardian ") has brought out one curious explanation of this sudden run on half-time certificates. It seems that there is some anxiety prevalent about the con- tinuance of the half-time system, and the fe3ling is that this may be the last chance parents will have of making money out of their children's labour. * *

This year will see the retirement of two soldiers who held prominent positions throughout the South African war, in the persons of Field-Marshall Lord Methuen and General Sir Neville Lyttleton. The former lays down the supreme command in South Africa early in April, while about a month later General Lyttelton hands over the com- mand of the forces in Ireland to General Sir Arthur Paget.ln each case their active career in the army will come to an end, though, nominally, Lord Methuen, being a Field- Marshall, remains upon the active list for life. He has been continuously in harness since the outbreak of the South African war, and it is understood he proposes to pass most of his time at his country seat, Corsham Court, near Devizes. * *

A woman correspondent of the "Manchester Guardian" has been interviewing the manager of big furnishing firm about modern waysi and current fashion. "The love of the home shows no sign of diminution, despite all rumours to the contrary,"was one of his sayings. "People are buying better stuff to-day than ever they did, and getting far better value for their money than five years ago. The change in the price of good furniture is one of the most striking features of our business. Wooden bedsteads have entirely ousted brass ones in up-to-date furnishing, and the • four-poster without hangings is coming much into fashion. Fashionable bedrooms are often furnished in highly polished grey wood, and glass-topped dressing tables are taking the place of the French-polished ones, which showed every mark and stain."

Russian merchants import from this county a supply of linen Piece goods. The protective duty. on some of these goods is nearly, eighteen pence a yard, or a tax equivalent to more than three times the value of the goods when they leave the hands of the British manufacturer. The manufac- turer sells at about 51d. a yard; the Russian 1 buys at about is. 11,1 d. a yard. Now, if the Russian Protectionists believe that the foreigner pays the tax (the foreigner in this case being the British exporter), how is it done? Can you find any man willing to pay a tax of eighteen pence out of fivepence half-penny? Perhaps a Tariff Reformer would do it, but it would be only to prove, heroically, in the face of facts, that his " argument " was correct. Argument is not arithmetic.

The memorial which Parliament decided to erect to Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman has been placed in the north aisle of Westminster Abbey, and was unveiled without ceremony yesterday. It consists of a bronze bust rather more than life size, and shows thenate Prime Minister in his robes of a Knight Commander of the Bath, and with notes in his hand. The sculptor, Mr. Paul Montford, has given to the features a characteristic expression—that blend of strength and geniality which made up a very pleasing countenance. The bust stands in a niche, on a pedestal of rouge antique marble, on which a simple inscription has been carved. At ten o'clock on Monday night, January Bth, three years ago, Sir Ernest Shackleton reached his farthest south, and, prevented by failure of the food supply from advancing, hoisted the Union Jack in latitude 88deg. 23min. S., within ninety-seven geographical miles of the pole itself. Nine weeks later, on March 23rd, 1909, the first news of his achievement came over the cables to London, and now we are waiting for the news that CaptainiScott has carried the flag over the last stage of the great ice plateau and placed it triumphantly at the southern apex of the earth's axis. Captain Scott calculated that with good luck, he would reach the Pole in Christmas week of last year, so that if all has gone well he is now on his way back with the last great prize of geographical exploration in his possession. Assuming the time-table was adhered to, the " Terra Nova" should be back at New Zealand early in March to cable home the results of the expedition.

A highly interesting lecture on " Rock climbin g' was given before the members of the Literary and Philosophical Society on Monday evening, by Mr. J. H. Melton, F.G.S , F.L.S., of Crosby. He pointed out that rock climbing was a blanch of mountaineering and the newest of all sports except aviation, which, until a short time ago, could hardly be called a sport, as it had a financial side, which no true sport should have. (Hear, hear and applause.) Rock climbing was a new sport and was not more than 30 years old; in fact, in the year IS3S "Murray's Guide to Sports- men" stated that it was a somewhat remarkable fact that a large proportion cf those who had ascended Mont Blanc " had been of unsound mind." (Laughter.) Of course, in rock climbing every possible precaution was taken by those in charge for the safety of those who made the ascents, which were by no means confined to "mere man." Solitary climbing was not to be encouraged, and parties generally consisted of three or four. Mr. Melton pointed out that rock climbing was essentially a summer sport, though operations in winter had an interesting side. Accidents occurred at times, but the history of all that had happened during the past twenty years or so showed that the climbers were doing something which they themselves would have condemned in others. It had been well said that the beginning of all wisdom and the root of all culture was to love the things we saw around us--the earth, the sea, the stars, the hues and forms of flowers, and the twilight on the hills. The call of Nature to the children of men had been finely said Out of the sound of the ebb and flow, Out of sight of camp and star, It calls you where the good winds blow, Where the unchanging meadows are ; From faded hops and hopes agleam, It calls you, calls you, night and day. Dr. Edgar Jones, M.R.C.S., who is England's, and probably the world's, oldest doctor, has just entered his 103rd year, at his residence, Great Burstead, in Essex. • DEATH OF MR. A. DUMBILL.--It is with the utmost regret that we publish the news of the untimely death of Mr. Albert Dumbill, of IVoolston, which occurred on Thursday night. For some weeks he bad been suffering from lung trouble but until hemorrhage set in on Thursday morning very few, if any, of his many friends anticipated so sudden and tragic a result. For several years the deceased had been preparing with characteristic eagerness for the profession of a school- master and bad successfully entered the Victoria University College for training. As a student at the Secondary School and Teachers' Centre his progress bad been very marked. On leaving the Padgate C.E. school only a few months ago for college the staff and scholars made him a present. In the midst of his scholastic work he had been an enthusiastic musician. During last summer he had obtained the diploma of A.L.C.M. For a number of 3 ears, even when quite a by, he acted as organist at the Wesleyan Church, Padgate, and a vesper he composed is there used regularly. In this capacity he had endeared himself to many friends who will feel his loss very keenly. A career that promised to be exceptionally brilliant has been closed, friends have lost one who was regarded by them with great affection, and mother and daughter are left to mourn the loss not only of a brilliant scholar and accomplished musican, but a noble and devoted son and brother.

VISIT OF THE REV. TREVOR H. DAVIES.—For FORlei time past, the members of the Wesley Guild had looked forward to the visit of the Rev. Trevor H. Davies, and on Thursday their anticipations of a great treat were fully realised. In the afternoon the rev. gentleman preached a most suggestive and eloquent sermon from the words, "Who touched Me." In the evening a large audience assembled in the schoolroom to hear his lecture on," The age of Chivalry." Nothing less than a verbatim report could do justice to the beauty (often epigrammatic) and mu,ic of the phrase- ology employed by the lecturer. Roughly speaking the lecture was based upon the vows by which knights of old pledged themselves at the altar, aud their application to present-day conditions. Speaking of the dragons of to-day Mr. D tvies referred to the "Curse of intoxicating drink," of the "Extravagance of wealth "as against "The Exigencies of poverty," of " Toe chill of avarice " and " The fever of amusement." He said the greatest knights of the moral world were all religious men and, as instances, quoted Cromwell, John Howard, Shaftesbury and Gladstone. Referring to the great need of true reverence in our day, the lecturer said that Greece and Rome fell by the sin of indolence and that the moralists of those ancient empires pleaded strongly against it. He quoted the case of the French Revolution in illustration of the effect of power in the , hands of a godless democracy. In connection with the knight's vow of loyalty to the King, the lecturer said that " Conscience is the Star of Bethlehem, that leadeth to the King," and that "Ethics 1033 themselve3 in religion." There was only one battle-cry that could possibly unite the different sections of the Christian army. and that was "Christas I mperatur." Councillor Henry Roberts, J.P., presided, and in response to a hearty vote of thanks to himself and the lecturer, said that an impious England would he a fallen England but that a sober and religious England would be the greatest England the world had ever seen.

It would not be merely a question of arithmetic but of kindly consideration towards the poorer nation. Ireland had undoubtedly been not only badly but unjustly governed by England in the past. Mr. Parker next touched upon the expensive character of the present methods of administration. The population of Ireland and Scotland was practically the same, yet the cost of constabulary in Ireland amounted to £1,481,000 as compared with £571,000 in Scotland. (A voice : " They don't want so much looking after in Scotland.") Yet the indictable offences in Scotland were more than double those in Ireland. (Ministerial applause). In Ireland the cost of police per bead of the population worked out at es. Bd., whereas in Scotland it was only 2s. 51d. (A voice : " Justified by results.") There was no country of the four com- prising the United Kingdom, in which there vets so little crime as in Ireland. (Applause.) The Government officials assessed for income tax' in Scotland numbered 938 and in Ireland 4,500. Their salaries totalled £1,435,000 in Ireland and £315,000 in Scotland. England spent in Government expenses one-fortieth of her national income, while Ireland spent one-tenth, thus baying to bear four times as much as England. The taxation of Ireland at the passing of the Act of Union was £2,500,000 ; at the present time it was £8,000,000, although the population had decreased by half. As showing the cumbersome system at present in force, Mr. Parker pointed nut that when a certain pier was constructed in the West of Ireland the cost of obtain- ing sanction from the authorities in London amounted to more than the actual cost of the structure itself. With regard to Ulster, be had travelled a great deal in that province and had found a considerable change in the attitude of the people with regard to Home Rule. The object of so ferocious a war cry is obviously to stampede the British electorate end it is well calculated to do so. Equality must le purged of ascendancy, and sentiment must be stripped of prejudice. The announced deterreina- t ion of a large number of hard-headed citizens led by a men of Sir E. Carson's standing to resist an Act of Parliament by force of arms may possibly persuade unthinking people that fiction is fact. But the device will fail. Mr. Parker concluded by expressing the hope that the Conservatives would not repeat the mistake they made with regard to the granting of self-government to South Africa, but would so consider the question that Home Rule would be given to Ireland as a boon not from a party but from a nation. Burglar-proof glass is now made in France. Embedded in the glass are light wires running in parallel transverse lines about one inch apart. The wires are con- nected to a battery, and carry a light charge of electricity. If the window is broken, the electric circuit is broken, and a bell is caused to ring. The breaking of the wires releases a magnetic switch, causing the alarm to be given. Unless the glass is completely broken no alarm will be given.

Some of the siren signal whistles now used for sea purposes consist of a disc having round holes or slits cut between the centre and circumference, which is caused. to whirl by steam pressure. There are two plates, the lower stationary and the upper revolving. When steam is turned on, the upper plate is revolved exactly as a windmill is Wawa round, and the faster it turns the more fre- quently the holes register, cutting off and passing the steam alternately. This causes vibrations of shorter and shorter period to be applied to the bell of the whistle, giving a higher and higher note, till the steam is cut off, when the note descends in the same way.

COLLISION WITH A COMET.

It appears that at one time a large comet did collide with this earth, doing, however, no particular damage. Geologists have reached the conclusion that the now famous crater near Coon Butte, Arizona, is the scar left by a great fall of meteoric matter; and the fact that seven of the ten largest known meteorites have been found within 900 miles of this place suggests that all have been scattered fragments from the same fall. They are similar masses of iron and nickel weighing from three to twenty tons each. Geological evidence indicates that the colli- sion occurred less than five thousand years ago; and stunted cedars growing in fba crater show by their annual rings that the time must have been at least feven hundred years ago, while annals of Cairo, Egypt, seem very convincingly to place the date in August, 1029. The records mention a great meteoric shower, when there was not only a brilliant light but a great noise, in contrast with the stillness of other such phenomena. EXERCISE IN BED.

Recent experiments have proved that die rays of radium constitute a stimulus to plant life. It being assumed that radio-activity is universally present in soil, water, rain, and snow, the conclusion is drawn that living matter can hardly escape its influence. It has been conclusively shown that a plant can be educated to endure an intensity of stimulus of this kind which at first retards its growth. Freshly fallen rain may have sufficient radio- activity to • retard the growth of plant organs, and so with tap-water which has pre- viously been exposod to the emanatioues of radium. THE STORAGE 01, COAL

Experiments have been made in Germany. says the "English Mechanic," with a view to ascertain the best means of preserving coal from deterioration after it had been mined. The coal experimented with consisted of i'-inch lumps, vessels of about half a gallon capacity being charged with it. The vessels were provided with air-tight covers and were filled either with water or with carbon dioxide, flue gases, or sulphurous acid vapours. Samples were taken and analysed after two weeks, three weeks, and six months. At the end of the latter pericd no further weathering seemed to occur. .t'arallel tests were made with coal exposed to the sir. The different sorts of coal did not all behave in the same manner, but, on the whole, it would appear that little is gained by keeping the coal in special atmospheres, or under water, though submarine storage ji as been reported as effective in other in- stances.

A TIE ON THE HOME RULE BILL.
Speaker gives Casting Vote In Favour.

Following the ChriEtruria holiday adjournment„ political warfare was resumed by the Warrington Parliamentary Debating Society on Tuesday evening when the concluding stage of the debate on the Home Rule Bill was reached. There was considerable excite- ment when, upon a division being taken, it was found that the House was equally divided on the measure. The Speaker (Mr. James Ball) e his casting vote in favour of Home Rule.

Mr. HARTLEY (C., Skipton), who re-opened the dis- cussion, opposed the Bill tor its non-utility. How WBB it going to benefit the great mass of the Irish popula- tion ? What were they going to receive that they did not get under the present administration ? Ile quite realized that there would he a great deal of benefit to Mr. John Redmond and a large number of other gentle- men. Probably he would want about £3,000 a year 1 salary and other Cabinet ministers would also have to be highly paid, but in what way would the scheme benefit the thousands of agricultural labourers who formed the great bulk of the population of Ireland? How, by giving a lot of politicians fat salaries, were they going to help the workers? He supposed Ireland would want to be self-support jog and would Dot care to take subsidies from England towards her maintenance. In that case, all the extra expense of carrying on the new Parliament would fall upon the Irish people. The Liberal party seemed to think that if they gave a country plenty of politics, it would mean more progress and comfort, but it often meant retrogression and unrest. That was what we were suffering from in England, and we did not want t inflict the same conditions upon Ireland. He did not consider that the troubles of Ireland were owing to the Act of Union. If that Act Lad never teen passed Ireland would have been worse off than she was to-day. During the last fifty years Ireland had gained by having a strong, rich and sympathetic nation to rely upon. Of course, the country had been badly used by England in days gone by, but never worse than by the great hero of the Liberal party—Oliver Cromwell. The troublous state of Ireland was not due to political but to geographical and economic reasons. The higher wages obtainable in Englatd and the United States accounted for the emigration of the best of the Irish people. Ile did not say that Ireland could be a rich country, but it could be contented and comfortable, unless it were cursed with Home Rule. The future of the country lay in developing its agricultural resources on a scientific basis and in distributing its produce economically and quickly. Mr. Boosev (L., Birkenhead), said the Home Rule Bill towered above all others, because it alone was the key to the peace and welfare of the Irish people. It would lessen the vast amount of labour and responsi- bility which devolved upon the Imperial Parliament and thus allow more time to be devoted to English measures. Ireland and England had very little in common. Schemes that would do for England would not do for Ireland, and how could the two countries work together amicably and peacably under the present conditions ? It had been said that Home Rule would mean Rome Rule. If so, why did a large number of leading Roman Catholic Peers oppose it ? Because they feared it would limit the powers of the Roman Catholic Church. Before the Act of Union, Ireland was prosperous, Lacing made rapid progress in agriculture and manufactures. It was not because Ireland was too poor to stend alone or that she was on the downward path to ruin that the union was brought about. It was incomprehensible why England should have deprived Ireland of her own control. Instead of advancing prosperity, it had robbed Ireland of all her gains. Having referred to the excessive burden of taxation which Ireland had been called upon to bear, the speaker said the education and land questions were entirely different in Ireland from the same questions in England, and Irish affairs could only be satisfactorily dealt, with by an Irish Parliament. Mr. C. PraesiroN (C., Darlington), said the Chief Secretary for Ireland, in introducing the measure, had dwelt too much upon the past history of Ireland, the bad laws under which she had suffered, and the despic- able methods by which the Act of Union was brought about. He did not think the House wenn derive any benefit from reaping up such con- siderations, especially when they recalled that for the greater number of years since the passing of the Act of Union the Liberal party had been in power and was equally responsible with the Tory Party for the bad laws enacted for Ireland. There was nobody on that side of the House but who deplored equally with members of other parties the mean and abominable methods that were adopted to bring about the Act of Union and he was convinced that his Nationalist friends would agree with him that since the Act was passed there had been a large number of people in Ireland who, through good and ill report, had constantly aimed at one object—to seethe Act repealed. It was the spirit of nationalism and he did not blame them for showing it. But when the Nationalists told us, as they were doing at the present time, that they were not aiming fer the repeal of the Act of Union, for an independent Parliament, or for separation from the United Kingdom,he said they were false to themselves. If they were animated by the spirit of nationality, they were no ration if they remained content with anything that would bind them to the United Kingdom. The speeches of Mr. Parnell, Mr. Devlin, Prof. Kettle, Mr. Redmond and other Nationalist leaders,when they were addressing their constituents in Ireland and their fellow-country men in the United States, were couched in a very different tone from that which they adopted on English platforms. Although it might defer for many years the attainment of their aspira- tions, it would be more honourable and fair to place their aims distinctly before the people of the United Kingdom. In their speeches at the present time the Nationalist leaders were trying to belittle their own party and their nation. If they were going in for a separate Parliament and nationality, they would be false to their principles if they accepted a Bill like the present one, which was an absolute absurdity. The omission of any reference to financial adjustments was sufficient to damn the whole Bill. He had spoken on many occasions in favour of Home Rule and he felt compelled, in justice to himself and in consistency wilh what be had said in the past, to vote against the Bill because be believed that, as it was drawn up, it would be injurious not only to England but to the United Kingdom and an insult to the Irish nation. Mr. C. E. PARKER (L, Dundee) said there were same arguments on which both Liberals and Conservatives could stand together. One was the question of the congestion of business in the Imperial Parliament. Undoubtedly our legislators were at present over- worked, and the measures which were passing through Parliament were not getting the time and attention they demanded. The guillotine might be a good thing to suppress those who would speak merely to defer legislation, but when there was a risk of the laws of the country not being properly considered, it became a danger. Moreover, the Imperial Parliament was not giving Imperial matters the attention they deserved. For instance, the Indian Budget was generally rushed through in about one night. He thought both parties also stood on the same platform with regard to the general principle that people managed their own affairs better than others managed them for them. Nothing was so educational as to let a child do a thing itself, and what was true of children applied universally to older people and to nations. CHESHIRE SCHOOL MANAGERS AND TEACHER SUED.

Before his Honour Judge Reginald Brown, K.C., and a jury at the Northwich C unity Court on Wednesday Joseph Astbury, 14, Gladstone-street, Northwicu, machine driller, brought an action on behalf of his daughter, BArbara Asbury, aged 11, for £2O medical expenses and damages against the Rev. Canon Binney (vicar of Northwich), the Rev. J. A. Dibben (vicar of Castle-Northwich), Joseph Naylor, Dr. H. E. Gough, J. W. Deakin, and William Thompson, all managers of the Castle Girls' School, and against Robina Wotheispoon, school t?.acher, The particulars of claim recited that on the 16 tb May last Barhara Astbury, while a scholar at the Castle School, was locked or fastened in a cupboard by Alias Wotherspoon, and that as a result of such improper punishment she wee taken ill. Mr. F. Brocklehurst appeared for the plaintiff, Mr. H. Hatt Cook for the managers, and Mr. J. H. Cooke (Winsford) for the teacher.

Mr. i3rocklehurst, in opening, said that up to May last Barbara Astbury was a bright and intelligent child, but highly strung. She was afflicted with a slight deafness, but had never been unwell. On the 16th May the entered tho school after play. A reading lesson had begun. The teacher was explaining the meaning of a word, and in order to catch the explanation the little girl stool up on the rear form. The moment she stood up she was ordered for punishment by the teacher, and instead of sending her to the headmistress, the teacher, Miss Wotherspoon, put the child into a cupboard under a staircise, and locked her up in what might be des- cribed as the Black Hole of Calcutta.
