div.head: FROM ' LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
div.p: FROM ' LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
By Philip Snowden, M.P.
THE POLITICAL ORGANISATION OF LABOUR.

At the German Reichstag elections, which are now taking place, the Socialists, who are the counterpart of the British Labour Party, will poll probably about 4,000,000 votes, and will return 80 to 100 members on a strictly independent ticket. The British Labour Party might do a less useful work than to make a very serious examination of the reasons for the great difference between the strength of the proletarian movement in Germany and: Great Britain. The British Labour Party is just now seriously taking in hand the question of the establishment of a daily Labour paper. The German Socialists run 82 daily papers, one of which has a circula- tion of 150,000 copies a day. The only political Labour and Socialist journal in this country, which has been established for nearly twenty years, has never paid its way, and its present circulation is little more than that of a prosperous local weekly newspaper. In membership also the British Labour and Socialist movement is sadly behind the continental movements. Last year the German Social Democratic Party increased its membership by three times more than the whole membership of all the Socialist organisations in Great Britain. The German Reichstag consists of 397 members, and at the present elections a Socialist candidate will be put forward in every constituency. The British Labour movement was content at the last election to contest less than one seat in twelve ; and at a recent bye-election in a great industrial centre, where Labour candidates had previously polled large votes, no Labour candidate was put forward, pre- sumably because the party could not find either a candidate or the money. The British Labour Party claims to have about 1,600,000 members affiliated to it, and it is not credit- able to the movement that its organisation should be in such an inefficient state. NO PROPER ORGANIZATION.

The British Labour Party has not won its successes by its organisation. It has won them in spite of the lack of organisation. It is a marvel that the party has polled such splendid votes when one knows how lacking the organisation has been. Take the last two by-elections fought by the Labour Party —Keighley and Oldham. In neither con- stituency was there any political organisa- tion. No attention had been given to the register, there was no party agent, there were no committees. The organisation had to be got together when it was decided to contest the seat. Very much the same applies to the constituencies where Labour has secured the Parliamentary representa- tion. In few of them is there any proper organisatitm. In some of them there is no organisation worth the name. The Labour Party has won its victories on enthusiasm, and because there is a large amount of unorganised sympathy in the industrial constituencies.

But the need for organisation increases as the party becomes more settled, because the virgin enthusiasm wanes, and the opposition becomes more determined. Unless the Labour Party turns its attention seriously to this question of organisation there is no prospect that it will materially increase its Parliamentary strength. The granting of Payment of Members has afforded the Labour Party an opportunity of doing something more thorough in the way of the organisa- tion of its forces Payment of Members has relieved the funds of the Labour Party to the extent of £B,OOO a year, and the funds of certain trade unions by an almost equal amount in the aggregate. This has set free money which should not be allowed to go back toi the affiliated societies, but should be used to make the party a greater power in the politics of the country. UNFAIR BURDENS ON A FEW.

The financial arrangements of the Labour Party have never been logically fair and defensible. The Labour Party is not really a party, but a federation of parties, and the constituent bodies have hitherto exercised the functions and borne the responsibilities which really belong to the Labour Party as a whole. For instance, the Labour Party does not promote candidatures. It only I endorses candidates which are put forward by affiliated bodies, which must accept the financial responsibility for the cost of the elections, the Labour Party giving a small I subsidy towards the cost. This has given rise to a good deal of unfairness and inequality of sacrifice. The Independent Labour Party is an affiliated body. Its membership is only about one- , third that of the Engineers' Society or of the I Railwaymen's Union. But the 1.L.P., as a rule, puts forward more candidates than these two societies put together. Then there are many unions affiliated to the Labour Party which do not promote a candidate at all, and therefore they contribute very little to the maintenance of the activities of the Labour movement. A small organisation like the I.L.P. has spent nearly .£20,000 on elections during the last six years, whereas some other bodies affiliated to the Labour Party have spent nothing. If the elected Labour members are to be regarded as belonging to the Labour Party as a whole, and if the Labour Party is to be able to claim their allegiance, then all the bodies affiliated to the Labour Party will have to bear a proportionate share of the expense of the electoral activities of the Party. It is not fair that such disproportionate burdens should be put upon certain con- stituent bodies. A trade union which bears the cost of an election, and 'the maintenance, maybe, of an organiser in the constituency, is really doing the work of the Labour move- ment as a whole, and it is not fair that it should have to meet practically all the expenses, while other unions escape financial contribution simply by doing nothing. Neither is it fair that an exceptional burden should be put upon the particular constitu- encies which are contested. The Labour , movement as a whole should bear, if not all, I at anv rate nearly all the cost of the election. In the case of the I.L.P. candidates, the con- stituency has to raise a good part of the cost of the election; and this is decidedly unfair, because the fact that there is a good Labour support in the constituency shows that the local organisation has done a great amount of propaganda work at its own cost. SOME MEAGRE PROPOSALS.

Tho Executive of the Labour Party had an opportunity to consider the whole situation in regard to the financial basis of the Party when the Payment of Members came into force. That concession, as has been said, relieved the Party funds to the extent of £B,OOO a year. The Executive have con- sidered the situation, and they are making certain recommendations to the Labour Party Conference which is to meet in Birmingham in a fortnight. But the recommendations of the Executive are paltry, and are quite unworthy of the

Labour Party. The contributions which affiliated bodies have hitherto paid to the central funds of the Labour Party are 15s. per 1,000 members for the general expenses of the office, and 2d. per member for the Parliamentary fund, out of which the allowance to M.P.'s and the subsidies to election expenses have been paid. This is the only contribution a great many unions have paid to the political work of the Labour movement, and surely no-one would maintain that it is too much. Instead of maintaining these contributions it is to be proposed to reduce them to id. per member. The new scale of payment will yield a sum of £5,000 a year, which it is estimated will meet the expenses of the Party. There will be tens of thousands of affiliated members who will Icontribute nothing beyond this id. a year. This is simply playing at politics. If it is not worth more than a penny a year to belong to the Labour party, the Party is not worth belonging to. The least that might have been suggested was that the old contributions should be maintained, and that the released funds should be employed to subsidise to a larger extent the societies who are doing active and expensive work for the movement as a whole. It is suggested that the reduced con- tributions will enable the centre to do more for the societies which are running candidates than has been done hitherto, now that the allowance to M.P.'s has not to be paid. So it is proposed to make grants to the localities which employ full-time organising agents, This is very good, and it will be a great help, and will probably lead to an addition to the number of such. But the central body should do more in the way of helping to pay the cost of elections, and it cannot do that out of the income it will have under the pro- posed scale of contributions. The sectionalism lof the Labour Party needs to be abolished. We do not want our Labour M.P.s to be candidates of a particular union or society, but the candidates of the National Labour movement. That can only be the case if the national movement accepts the financial responsibility for the candidatures. It can never afford to do that out of an income of Id. a member per year. A penny a year to a national Labour Party!

HOW THE ANIMALS CHOOSE AIKING. This week I am going to tell you an ancient fable, which all clever boys and girls will be able to interpret for themselves. A FABLE. The lion was dead, and all the animals ran to his lair to sympathise with the lioness, his widow, who was making the woods and mountains resound with her cries. After they had expressed their regrets to her at the death of her husband, they began the elec- tion of a king, the crown of the dead king being placed in the midst of the assembly. The lion's whelp was too young and too weak to obtain command over so many wild animals. "Allow me to think," said he, "that I shall know how to rule well and to cause myself to be feared. Whilst waiting, I wish to study the gallant deeds of my father, that I may one day equal him in renown," "As for myself," said the leopard," I lay claim to the crown, because I am more like the lion than all the other claimants." "And I," said the bear, "maintain that an injustice was done to me, when the lion was chosen instead of me; I am strong, brave and a flesh cater just as the lion; and I have a singular advantage, as I climb trees." "I leave you to judge, gentlemen," said the elephant, "if anyone can dispute with me the fame of being the largest, the strongest, and the bravest of animals." " I am the noblest and the most beautiful," said the horse "And I the most cunning," said the fox. " And I the swiftest in the chase," said the stag._

"-Where will you find," said the ape, "a more agreeable and ingenious king than me? I shall amuse my subjects every day. lam like man, who is the true king of nature." The parrot next addressed the animals : "Since you boast of resembling man, I can boast also. You are only like him in your ugly face and in your ridiculous grimaces; as for me, I resemble him in my voice,which is the mark of reason and the best ornament of man." " Be quiet, stupid *chatterer," replied the ape ; " you talk, but not like man ; you always say the same thing without under- standing what you say." The assembly laughed at the two bad imitators of man, and they gave the crown to the elephant, because he had strength and wisdom, without having either the cruelty of fierce beasts or the foolish vanity of •so many others who always wish to appear what they are not. THE SEVEN STARS INN.
THE END OF A FAMOUS HOSTELRY.

The most familiar of Manchester's old buildings is in the bands of the destroyer and the " Seven Stars" will soon be passed from view. The old place had a fairly firm hold upon the affections of Manchester people,and we are surprised that they feel able to part with it.

Twenty years ago a local writer said "The Seven Stars has a thoroughly respectable standing, and however it may be over- shadowed, it will take a pretty broad extinguisher to snuff it out." But the extinguisher has come. The " Magpie " walls and gables must give place to moun- tains of terracotta, and the antiquarian must write his rueful valedictory.

div.head: SEVEN STAR MYTHS:
div.p: SEVEN STAR MYTHS:
The first thing is to rid the building of a cluster of myths. It is the kindest thing,too, for a pretty sample of Elizabethan architecture needs no help from ignorant my th- mongers. _
W 0 begin with that which for years has been blazoned upon its sign,
THE OLDEST LICENSED -HOUSE IN GREAT BRITAIN. LICENSED OVER 540 YEARS. _ _

The credulity of mankind is great, and words so boldly displayed have been accepted by scores of sober writers. Only a few weeks ago Manchester's enlightened and welt- informed antiquarian paper,the "City News," solemnly said that "as the oldest public-house in Great Britain it has been associated with the social and political doings of this country for over 550 years . . • . that through a subterranean passage from the inn to the

Cathedral, Guy Fawkes escaped from King James' soldiers . . . that a regiment of King Charles soldiers left a set of mess plate there, which was discovered, all black with age, in the wall some years ago." This string of statements, however attrac- tive to the imagination, contains not a fragment of known truth. No student of architecture would place the date of the fabric further back than 400 years and it may be of later date than that. The statement as to the license is an absurdity, for licenses were unknown 540 years ago, and the very earliest mention of such a thing belongs to the year 1552. Before that date any householder could sell ale. In Manchester in the sixteenth century anyone was allowed to keep an inn and brew and sell intoxicants, provided they could also provide two beds for the accommodation of travellers.. Not until 1579 did licensing in any form come into operation in the town on the Irwell, and the "Seven Stars" is not mentioned for a long time after that. The secret passage leading to the Cathedral has never been seen by any responsible person, and the stories about it are pure romance.

Nor is it true that Guy Fawkes lay con- cealed in what is known as "Ye Guy Faux Chamber," though Harrison Ainsworth does try hard to make us believe it. The yarn about the mess plate might have passed for genuine, but some expert got a glimpse of it, and reported that though very black it was not black with age, and that it was of Brittania metal stamped with the rather modern inscription "Dixon and Son, Sheffield."
Thus faded another myth, and visitors have not in recent years been encouraged to ask to see this supposed relic of the Civil War. WHAT OUGHT TO HAVE BEEN.

But we must not be severe upon the inventors of these stories. They evidently felt that all sorts of romantic things ought to have happened there. The rooms'are so very ancient in their flavour, the old beams and pannelling so eerie and time-worn that we refuse to believe they have had only an ordinary history. Ideally many things ought to have happened here. Spencer should have spent a night and added a chapter to his " Fairie Queen " : Walter Raleigh ought to have slept in the Guy Fawkes chamber and left his initials on the window pane; Shakespeare ought to have had a ihappy night with Ben Jonson and then dreamed new things for his "Merry Wives of Windsor " ; and Queen Elizabeth might have'done worse than honour the "Seven Stars," for she slept in many a worse place, if some legends be true. _

The veriest dullard— sitting in the "Seven Stars " will agree that all these things ought to have happened. The pity is they didn't. But local imagination has done its best, and the fixing up of Guy Fawkes at the "Seven Stars" was really good.

Leaving the things which busy brains have woven, it is worth while to attempt a real picture. And this, by the aid of estate records is possible. We are back in days of Queen Elizabeth. What is now Withy Grove was known as Withingreave, a pleasant country lane with a babbling brook. This gives the name Withingreave, and the builders gather the withies to plait and daub with cla_y between the timbers of their houses. "

There were many callers at the big house in those days; and everyone who saw Sir Gregory left no doubt as to their satisfac- tion. The condolences upon the death of the daughter were few and formal compared with the sincerity of the congratulations on the score of Bulmer's future.

And every word of the kind that was spoken went like a sworti stab to Sir Gregory's heart, and added to the difficulty of breaking his long silence. He accepted the hearty wishes of his friends day by day without a protest; but every night resolved that the next day should see the end of the hollow sham, while every morning found him weakly postponing the ordeal. The marriage with Mrs. Caulfield, which he had striven so earnestly to promote and had hoped for so heartily, was now as dis- tasteful to him as it had formerly appeared desirable; and in his eager anxiety to escape the shame of avowing the truth, he began to consider whether, after all, his confession was necessary. Helen was married and presumably happy in America with her husband. To restore her her birthright meant the disinheriting of his son and an old age of infinite trouble and sorrow and shame for Lady Trevellock. The innocent would be punished, and no one would gain except the man who had mar- ried Helen—an Aracrican millionaire, who would no care for the ~.as , and to whom it would be no mote than a superfluous adjunct to his already enormous wealth. Ought he to beggar his wife and son in order to add to the riches of a man already over- burdened with wealth? It was right and legal, of course; but was It necessary? If Helen had been in need, it would have been a different thing. But now she would never miss the inheritance of which she had never known. There was another consideration, too. She had ap- peared to care for Bulmer, and having so much of her own, she would probably prefer to let him keep the Chase. There WAS but one barrier to continued silence—Jasper Bostock. But even he did not know that Helen was the child of that first marriage. Sir Gregory had questioned him now and again sufficiently to see that. All he knew was the other secret—that old affair with Jake Stevens; and he had been contented hitherto with the money paid him to hold his tongue. He could probably be kept silent by the same means. If Bostock had known of Helen's identity, it would have been different; or if he had known where to find her, and so possibly pierce her secret. But the price paid for the smaller secret Iliad been liberal; and Bos- tock was not the man to talk when silence paid him so well. With such considerations as these, al- though tortured intermittently with the pricking of his unquiet conscience' Sir Gregory put off the ordeal and tried to justify to hims2lf the course which he was so desirous to adopt; and at the same time sought to ascertain Bulmer's real feelings in regard to Mrs. Caulfield. ' Did you ever speak to Mrs. Caulfield about Mr. Bostock, Bulmer?" he asked one

40h, yes. I was altogether wrong. He is a man of high character and position. She line known him for years, father. Grainger must have spoken out of spite." "A man of high character," repeated Sir Gregory in surprise. "Did she say how she had come to know him and what she knew?" "I did not press it, of course, -when shp spoke so highly of him." No, no. Of course not." He spoke some- what absent-mindedly, for it had just occurred to him as a strange thing that she should know a man of Bostock's character, and give him such praise. Almost enough to engender a doubt about herself. "How are things 'getting on in regard to your mar- riage?' . "All right, sir. There's only another fort- night now. Beth says she'll be ready, although it's a bit of a scramble." "There's not so much need for haste as thcre was. You might put it off for a while. Perhaps she would rather delay it. Women like to make a splash at such a time." "I don't think she would. And so far as I am ooncerned one time is as good as another," he added, with a shrug of the shoulders. • "That's scarcely how one expects a man to speak of his wedding, Bulmer." "I am afraid it's just about how I feel, sir. I'm sorry for it, of course; but we all know that it isn't exactly a wedding -of that sort. You wished it, and my mother is very anxious about it, and, of course, Beth herself understands how it is. I explained all that when I asked her to marry pie. She's a bright, good little soul, and I hope I shall be able to make her happy. But we don't pre- tend that it is a conventional love match." "Do you think it would be wiser to post- pone it? Lotta's death is so recent, and under such circumstances everyone would understand." "But you have wished it so much, sir," replied Bulmer, surprised at the change of mind the remark appeared to indicate. "I am only thinking of your happiness, my boy." Bulmer smiled rather sadly, and shook his head. "I'm afraid it's rather too late even to postpone it. My word is passed, father ;" and with a half smothered sigh he went

away. The conversation troubled him. It had served to put into definite shape the vague, restless thoughts which had been plaguing him since Lotta's death. He did not wish to marry Mrs. Caulfield. He had been hurried into the proposal by the failure of the life assurance office, and his father's fears for the future. If he had only waited, the need for haste would hive passed. He did nbt wish to marry anyone. Now that he could look forward to becom.

ing the owner of the Chase, it would have been infinitely better for all if he remained unmarried. He had not forgotten Mrs. Caul- f, field's kindness and sympathy in the days of 1, his trouble in regard to Helen' nor that the G companionship with her had been pleasant ;. and grateful. He owed her m real debt of rk gratitude on that account. But the days of his engagement had been a trial and a weariness. He discovered that the very subject which had then been a sort of bond between them was now an actual 14 bar. He could not talk to the woman he was going to marry about the woman to whom he had given his love; the love of his life. Nor would he pretend to make love when he felt none. He had explained everything frankly, but it was one thing to make an explanation ind another to live constantly up to the con- ditions which it imposed. None the less, he was bound by his word and by his honour. Mrs. Caulfield had con- sented to marry him when he had had no- thing; and now that he was to have the Chase he could not turn round -and renounce her. He was bound to marry her, but the obligation chafed and galled him Sorely. He was pacing the grounds in the maze of these unpleasant thoughts when Mrs. Caul- field came suddenly upon him from side natb where she had becii in waiting. The

raugh with which -she pounced out upon him grated and jarred. "What a frown, Bulmer," she jested. "And how solemn you look. You might be thinking out a speech in readiness for .your Parliamentary dap." They had spoken of his intention to enter Parliament. "I was not expecting to see you, or I should have had a smile ready, Beth." "Now that's real pretty. But you didn't smile when you said it, you know. What were the black thoughts about?"

"Nothing—at least, no, nothing." "Then they weren't about me? Anyway; I hope they weren't, for I shouldn't -like to bring such a frown to your face. 11 I have my way life shall be one long smile for us both. There's no reason why it shouldn't be, is there?" "I shall always try to make you happy, Beth. You deserve it."

She slipped her hand into his arm and turned to walk with him. "Tell me what you were frowning about, dearest. I want to share the shadow as well as the sunshine. And you were frowning. Has anything hap- pened—anything unpleasant, I mean?" "No. Nothing unpleasant exactly. I've been talking with my father; and it set me thinking. That's all. "I haven't seen Sir Gregory for two or three days. I half feared he had been avoid- ing me. There cannot be any reason for that, can there?"

"I can't see any—unless, perhaps, it's about Mr. Bostock. He sticks to it that the man is no better than he should be; but 1 told him what you had said, and it may be that, holding to his opinion, he thinks it strange you should have been so certain that Bostock is all right." "Why has he taken ilea pejudice so sud- denly? Mr. Bostock has been coming and go- ing here for months, and slways at Sir Gre- gory's own invitation." "I told him that was what poor Lotta had said, but he explained it in a way. He knew Bostock in the old days, it seems, out in the. West, and knew nothing good of him. If Lotta had not died, my father meant to stop that marriage, lie told rue 80, and was quite bitter about it."

"Then why have him hem?" "I don't really know," replied Bulmer, a little impatiently. "I gathered something to the effect that Bostock knew something which my father did not wish generally known, and thought it best to be civil to him."

Mrs. Caulfield shrugged her pretty shoul- ders and deemed it best to drop the subject. St4e, remembered how Bostoek had often spoken of his hold over Sir Gregory, and was quick enough to perceive how strange her own statements about the man might appear to Sir Gregory. "I suppose there is no chance of your being mistaken about him, Beth?" he asked after a pause. "It might be a rather serious thing for me if I were, Bulmer. But you remember my promise to write out to Denver. I have written, but, of course, there has not been time to hear yet. But it can't have been that which made you look so troubled just now?" "You are determined to have it, eh? Well, Sir Gregory thinks that the date for our marriage is a littie soon afterAotta's death." "I'm glad that made you 4olemn, dearest," she replied quickly and with intentional mis- understanding. "It shows that you doo't agree with hirn, and are as eager for our marriage as I am. 'Oh, I am counting the very hours, Bulmer." Ire winced. "Of course. I told him so," he answered, suppressing a sigh of regret. "I'm getting everything ready splendidly," she went on, affecting not to notice his man- ner. "I've had to get a hustle on, as we say; and I've cabled out to Denver that my people-are to make things hum in readiness for us. I think you will just love my home out there ;'.' and she drew him on this way to speak of America and their plans for the trip they were to make in the States. "No. There's no hope of doing anything," lie said to himself when she had left him. shall have to go through with it. Well, she's a goad little soul and " he smothered a sigh of bitter regret and left the thought un- spoken. Two days later, Bosteek returned unex- pectedly. ,Bulmer received him very coldly, but, for Mrs. Caulfield's sake, not uncivilly; and to his surprise, he found the two in close consultation more than once. She explained this once by saying that Bostock had been engaged about some of her affairs. "They appear to be troublesome affairs, Beth," he answered lightly. "I have never seen you look more worried than when I came on you two this afternoon." "It is only some mining business, Bulmer. But nothing of real importance." "Who is the Mr. Garwood whose name I caught as I came into the room? I couldn't help hearing the name." "A New York lawyer who is handling some of my affairs," was the glib reply. "I am sorry you have any bothers," he answered; and the matter passed. But the next day when he went into his father's study he found Bostock there. The man seemed always talking secrets, he thought, seeing that both of them appeared uneasy at his entrance. As a matter of fact Sir Gregory had just been giving Bostock some money, and was afraid that Bulmer had seen it. Bostock, seeing that matters were begin- ning to go wrong with him had made a much heavier demand than usual, to be prepared for eventualities, and Sir Gregory had been greatly upset by Bostoek's attitude. For the rest of the day he was troubled and very nervous. And Bulmer noticed this.

He grew convinced that there was some- thing under the surface which he did not understand; and during the night resolved to question his father. It was insufferable that a man like Bostock should be swagger- ing about the Chase in this way. With all this in his mind, he went to Sir Gregory directly after breakfast on the fol- lowing morning. "I want to talk to you about that fellow Bostock, father," he be-
gin. "I can't understand him, and I don't like him to be here."
"He has done a little business for me, Bul- men A rather unpleasant business in which a London solicitor is concerned—a Mr. Gar- wood."

"What name?" cried Bulmer. "A London solicitor, you say?" Garwood was the name of the man Mrs. Caulfield had been discus- sing with Bostock. What could it mean? "Yee. But it's nothing. I've arranged it," replied Sir Gregory. As he was speaking a servant entered with the postbag. Ile welcomed the interruption; and opening the bag handed over to Bulmer the one or two letters addressed to him.

There was nothing of importance in them, and he was skimming them through when Sir Gregory uttered a sudden, sharp cry, pressed his hand to his heart, and leant back in his chair, gasping as if in difficulty for breath. Rising in quick alarm Bulmer went to his assistance, and as he reached him his eyes fell on the address and the opening sentence of the letter which his father had just opened. 'I am writing you in regard to Miss Helen Powell, or Paxton. . . . Impulsively he drew the paper from his father's trembling grasp and laid it on the edge of the tab!e beyond his reach. At the same instant Sir Gregory regained his self-command, and, as Bulmer turned, their eyes met. , • IT6' tie continued.)

"RING THE BELL, WATCHMAN." Uncle Caleb's last week's story reminded me of a very similar one f a small boy who was evidently desirous of knccking at the door of a large house, but was tco short to rea:h the instrument. Observing this, an eminent ecclesiastic who happened to be pass- ing gave a resounding rat-tat-tat for him, whereupon the mischievous youngster took to his heels, recom- mending the friendly cleric to do the like if he did not want to get into hot water! That in turn recalls the one about the little girl at the village school who, on being spoken to by an aristocrath visitor, neglected the formalities demanded by etiquette on such occa- sions. The horrified teacher whispered "You must say Your Grace,'" and the simple youngster imme- diately folded her hands and with bowed head murmured "For what we are about to receive may the Lord make us truly thankful!" MORE SLIPS. In last week's "Notes and Notions " it was told how, as a member of Parliament, an Irish County Court Judge once addressed the Speaker as" Y ur Revererce. ' /in old solicitor ef my acquaintance, who has a considerable practice in advocacy,habitually makes such blunders, constantly addressing the County G urt Judge as " Your Worship," and the presiding magistrate at the Police Court, as " Your Honour." However, even great Homer nods. Not long ago, Mr. Birrell declared from his place in the H use of Commons that a newspaper account of a certain Incident was " a wholly garbled version of what never took place." To be sure, be was speaking as Chief Srcretary for Ireland. Now !hat we have reached tho centenary of the great novelist's birth, Dickens orations are the or der of the day. One speaker on the prevailing topic is reported as saying that what made Charles Dickens great was that he spoke to the common heart of humanity, and the sirorci he had drawn against social abuse was still ploughing its way towards the goal he had set himself to reach. The italics are mine. After all, 'tis but a case of turning sword into ploughshare, and we are bound to believe there is a good time coming when that will Le common. PANTOMIME.

This week's panto at the Palace remimls me that the institution is well nigh a couple of hundred years old, for it was on Boxing Day in 1717 that John Rich produced his "Harlequin Executed" in London. I read that the pantomimes of the eighteenth century told a serious story, despite the comic incidents, and Rich gave the "property man " his chance to produce wonderful stage effects. Ho and his company moved to Covent Garden in 1732, and then the public were treated to splendours in the way of fl)ing chariots, triumphal cars, palanquins, wickerwork lions, pasteboard swans, &c., Soc. For some time the Harlequin was reckoned the principal personage, but, as my authority puts it, the sceptre was wrested from that masked and lozenge-patterned personage by that Lest of all clowns, Joseph Grimaldi, who used to draw big houses and have " bumper bend's " at Liverpool's Theatre Royal. Before he was fifty years of age he retired from the profession, a prematurely aged man, for he had worked too hard at the business of making people lauA,h. He systematically played at two theatres a Inight, and sositetimes even three, and even "the genuine droll, the grimacing, filching, irresistible clown " could not stand many years of this. Ile left the stage in 1828, and died nine years later. When I was a yonagster,Harry Bolen° was a noted clown, and [think I have previously mentioned in this column,the late Wilson Barrett's brother George played the same pait in Christmas pantomime; but old Joe Grimaldi has never been rivalled. Now the chalked and raddle- faced clown, the fish-scaled harlequin with wooden sword, the lean and slippered pantaloon, and the fairy- like Columbine have disappeared, the harlequinade, which of old was the chief feature of the pantomime, has disappeared altogether. These personages used to have places in the opening of the pantomime, and at the transformation scene were themselves trans- formed under the influence of the fairy's wand in the presence of the audience, their outer clothes going down traps. I give this explanation because the younger generation knows nothing of these things. The other evening I spent an hour in a "picturedri me," and there was a representation of the old-fashioned harlequinade, but the young folk who were present could make nothing at all of it. " What are they supposed to be doing ? " asked one h red ftllow of his companion. " Nay," was the reply of the equally puzzled mate, " I can't tell what this is about. I never saw or heard of anything like this before ! " Ab, well ;.other times other manners. Nowadays the scenic artist, carpenter, and costumier are allowed greater latitude in money spending,and stage splendour has developed to an extent undreamt of in the reign of Rich At the same time, fun permeates the while piece ; and I for one do not regret the supersession of the ancient clown with Lis red hot poker, stolen sausages, unhealthy humour, and lax moral code. WHAT TO AVOID.

_ About the time that the medical paper cited in a note in these columns a week ago published that paragraph as to the cause of one's hair changing colour, I heard a mother who had been summoned for not sending her little girl to school plead in all apparent honesty that the child had been so terrified by the preliminary proceeding that her hair bad turned white! The chief lesson of the item quoted in last Saturday's " Examiner " seemed to be that one should wear a loose collar. Let me add the warning that it should not be of celluloid. In one of my visits to the Royal Eya Hospital in Oxford-road, Manchester, I found among the in-patients a boy. who,througb the accidental firing of such dangerous neckwear, had been permanently disfigured. He was lucky to have escaped with his life; before and since, many deaths have occurred as the result of similar mishaps—in fact, there have been two or three such during the last fortnight. TWELFTH NIGHT.

This, of course, is the twelfth after Christmas Day. Of the customs that long hung about it, but have gradually died out, some of the moat striking sprang out of the old belief teat the Magi, who visited the Bethlehem manger and offered their gifts, were no less personages than Melchior, who presented the gold, Jaspar, who offered incense, and Baltasar, whose gift was myrrh, three kings of Colon, out from Arabia, then styled the East by dwellers on the Levant Selden tells how the custom of choosing kings and queens on Twelfth Night sprang up amongst the aristocracy of this country. The Twelfth Night Cake was the vehicle through which each festive party choose a king and a queen. Secreted in the cake were both a bean and a pea. The gentleman in whose slice the bean was found was at once rroclaimed the King of the Bean, and the lady in whose share of the cake the pea turned up, was Queen. The custom i obtained n this country to such an extent that in Queen Elizabeth's progress through the land, dialogues and poems were recited before her referring directly to the cutting of the Twelfth Night Cake, and the selection of king and queen by the agency of the bean and pea. HOME SWEET HOME—MORE OR LESS! Fearing for the stability of the English home, I had somehow come to associate the decay of the sentiment of domesticity with the women's suffrage movement As a matter of fact, I had repeatedly heard lady advocates of what they term emancipation talk on public platforms as though the woman who remained at home and looked well to the ways of her own household were a slave to be pitied. Moreover people are writing in the newspapers as if the family bond had grown weaker and marital relations more brittle, and as if the beautiful dependence and mutual consideration once common in town and countly home-circles were degenerating into relations ef personal convenience, lightly assumed and often tragically sundered. Indeed, I fancy the impression as to this was so general that it might be taken for granted. The Rev. F. B. Meyer, who has of late bulked largely in the public eye, suggests among other causes for the " slackness of home ties," that "the women of the present day, whose presence is the main attraction and bond of the home life, have emerged from the seclusion in which they were formerly immured, and have entered into competition—with men in business and pastime." Happily, much error is mixed up with all this. Things are not really what they seem. Besides, even if an odd Mr. Jellaby here or there has to look after the home what time his better half (or, if you will, superior threequarters) is out tub-thumping about votes for women, that is as it shouli --but there ! This is a brick- lined pit fitted with ten carrying wheels that can be adjusted to any distances, and connected with much ingenious machinery that registers all that is worth knowing about a railway engine. The engine is run on to a table and lowered by sixteen screw- jacks on to the wheels of the tester, and the drawbar hook is hitched on to the dynamometer so that it cannot get away, although it is hauling at it all the time as if it were a train ; and the pull of the drawbar and the speed of the carrying wheels give the measure of power. The engine cannot move ahead, but it is started just as if it could, and quickly working up into speed, as if it were leaving a station, faster and faster it goes, until the noise is appalling. A 4-coup'ed engine running at seventy miles an hour and not moving an inch is a sight not easily forgotten. The engine is not run to waste, for the carrying wheels drive an air compressor that supplies the pneumatic tools. Not only are the measurements taken o: speed and power; the coal burnt and the water evaporated are accurately noted, and the chimney delivers into a box that forms a receptacle for ashes and anything else ejected by tho engine, all of which are examined and reported on. Blouses and Conts.—Tbis winter the three-piece frock—that is the skirt signally high waist ed with a dainty and elaborate blouse to match the dress in colour, and coat of the same material as the skirt—or otherwise if preferred—is very popular with women who dress really well. The blouse that can be worn with any odd skirt one may happen to possess, is no longer patronized by the fashionable individual. Shirts of the tailored and severely plain variety are however still worn with tweed and other suits. A glance at the shop windows is sufficient to prove that the woven woollen coat has almost entirely displaced tho hand- knitted and crocheted articles, that were so much in evidence last winter. And it must be confessed that the former possesses advantages over the latter. Then the shot effects are altogether alluring, and these have been very successfelly introduced in the woollen materials for spring wear. Gloves and Footgear.—Gloves and shoes were formerly—and by many persons are still—considered the hallmark of good tiste. Perhaps the endless varieties of make and colour—many of which may be characterised as freakish —to be seen in shopland nowadays, bewilder purchasers, and lead to a choice that spoils an otherwise pleasing tout en6onble. Wherefore, charming as are some of the coloured shoes, more especially those in surSde, which is so essentially effemenine, black shoes are always a safe purchase, because they go with any toilette. Many well-dressed women are showing a penchant for a black shoe of good make, natural in shape, and unobtrusive in appearance. Quite ideal is a black glace Oxford shoe, but it must be elegant in design and cut, and have no toe-cap, and its weight must fall naturally on the heel and ball of the foot. Leap Year.—Sentiment and respect for old customs play but a small part in modern life, and the woman of to-day scarcely knows of the special privileges afforded her by leap year. If the calendar reformers had their way, there would be an end to the tradition and if all the social reformers were squally triumphant, the occasion for its observance would vanish, because we should have equality of the sexes in matrimonial affairs, as well as in everything else. Under the suggested • calendar changes, we should have a fixed Easter, and four quarters of 91 days each in the year. New Year's Day would be neither a day of the week, or uf the month. It would be a day apart a universal holiday, and the next day would be January Ist. Leap year woull be provided for by a Leap Year Day, interpolated between June 30th and July Ist. That too would be a general holiday, so that people with fixed salaries would not have to work an extra day for nothing as many will this year. There a:e various reasons why it is called leap year, the one most generally accepted being that it is because the Doruinical Letter leaps a day, no letter being officed to February 23th, 'lke Week-end Habit.—" Week-ending "is credited with having brought about many social changes, within a comp tratrvely short time, for less than twenty years ago, the meaning of the phrase," week-end," as applied to visiting, was unknown, except in the North. In London, the "week-ender " was regarded very much as a " tripper " hut nowadays the week-end visit is both popular is fashionable. It belongs to an age in which everything s fast and furioul, and whilst there is no doubt that it has greatly changed Sunday habits, it is not without its influence upon the moderate con- ception of friendship. In the old-fashioned leisurely days, people went on lengthy visits to a friend's house and there was time for an acquaintance to develop into a real and lasting friendship. In these days of week- end visits there are few such opportunities. Yet although old friends are hest we need new ones. As people got on in life it is necessary to renew one's stock of friends as it is to renew the household furniture and linen. If we fail to take a keen interest in life and make no new friends we, like the home, will the more show signs of the wear and tear of passing years. Athletics and Woman's Physique.—Nothing is more striking than the superior stature of the twentieth century girl, as compared with the physique of former generations. It begins in infancy, for we are told that babies are bigger and heavier than babies used to be, and that it is not unusual to find them half as heavy again 89 the average weight in times gone by. This seems to be a good augury for a coming race of giants, but the modern girl, with her mannish propensities is not without critics. Every now and then we have an A.R.A. complaining that it is impossible to find a figure comparable to the Venus of Milo, and difficult to secure a model of normal feminine proportions. The modern girl with her taste for athletics and physical training, has shoulders too broad, waist too largo, and amongst other unseemlinesses she:shows hard muscles where there ought to be soft curves. However this may be from the artist's point of view, physical health and strength is to be preferred to the doll-like effeminacy of mid-Victorian times, and it may be questioned whether it is not altogether a myth to suppose that ordinary physical exercise conduces to feminine disfigurement. Some of the most beautiful figures may be seen among out stage dancers, whose whole life is spent in training, and there can be no question that the moderh taste for physical exercise has helped not a little to improve the general standard of the feminine stature. Tight Neckwear.—New discoveries of the cause of baldness, are almost as numerous as its supposed remedies, and a London doctor attributes it largely to the wearing of tight collars. If that were really so, there would be more baldness among women than men, for they are much more addicted to the use of tight neckwear. We are warned of many evils resulting from this habit, which is said to produce indigestion, headaches, faintness, and besides these and other ailments a sallow complexion and faded hair. We need not attach too much Importance to these warnings, because few, if any women are so foolish 83 to con- strict the neck so uncomfortably as to produce such results. At the same time, one can readily understand that tight neckwear is not conducive to the general health', but so long as it does not interfere with local circulation, that is all we need be careful about. " Prayers for a Statesman." At the Executive Committee of the Lancashire County branch of the National Service League, at Preston, on Tuesday, Major Strachan intimated that, as a result of the Home Rule campaign, the League could not get any speakers, and the proposed big meetings at Manchester and Liverpool had fallen through. Mr. Townroe (Warrington) said the outlook for big meetingsoas practically Lopeless, and it was decided to let them fall through. The reports of the organising secretary and the general treasurer showed that 432 meetings had been held during the year ; but, although they had had a donation of £2O(/ from headquarters, they had only a balance of UN,

Major Strachan drew attention to the allegations of General French with regard to the League's agents hampering the recruiting to the Territorial Army, and shid that the very opposite had been the case In Lancash i re.

_ Judge Hans Hamilton (who presided) said the League had done an enormous service in Lancashire, where they had an enormous field to work in. With regard to the statement that the League were hindering the progress of the Territorial Army, he was pretty certain that was the work of an enemy or the League. As a matter of fact, mem'iers of the Territorials were influential members of the League, and 91 per cent, of the members of the County Association of Lancashire Territorials were supporters of the National Service League. Last year thousands of people felt so strongly that the persons responsible for the safety of the women of the country were not doing rightly that they prayed day and night to Almighty God t 3 send a states- man to come forward and reveal the true state of affairs as githered from the information at the Admiralty and War Office, and that he would take adequate means to maintain and protect this country from the attacks of other nations. God answered their prayers so far as peace was concerned, but their prayers for a statesman had not been answered yet. If only men and women knew the true state of affairs they would insist on there being adequate provisions for the defence of the Kingdom. (Applause).

VERDICT OF SUICIDE AT CHESHIRE INQUEST. The inquest was concluded at Asbton-on-Mersey, on Tuesday, on Major Wood (53), civil and mining engineer, formerly of Newfield!, tymm. At the previous bearing it was stated that the major left home on Saturday morning, December 16th, and returned late at night, after spending the day in Manchester. Unable to secure admittance to the house, he tried to sleep in a brougham in the ccacbhouse, but eventually roused his srn. On entering the house Major Wood went into his study. Next morning he was found dead in the lavatory. The adjournment of the inquiry was made in order that an analysis of the contents of the stomach might be obtained, a medical witness stating that he was unable to state the cause of death. Mrs. Wood said that latterly her husband had been pressed financially. his nerves were highly strung. though she only kr ew during the last fortnight of his life that be suffered from insomnia. She id not know Ihe took chloridine, and he never expressed any inten- tion of taking his life. The Coroner now read the report of Mr. Carter Bell, the county analyst, who made an analysis upon the con- tents of the organs of deceased, and also open the contents of the bottles found on the premises. One of the bottles contained whisky and water and eleven grains of hydro cyanide of potassium (prussic acid), and the stomach and other organs contained sufficient of this poison to have caused death. Another bottle contained a proportion of alcohol and a quantity of carbonate of lime. Answering the Corr ner, Dr. Scott, who attended Major Wood, said the alcoholic liquor containing the carbonate of lime might have been taken by the deceased for indigestion, but it was an unusual thing to take. The Coroner : Then, doctor, would anyone take prussic acid for insomnia or highly-strung nerves ?—No, I don't think so. The jury returned a verdict of "Suicide during a fit of temporary insanity.

In the course of his annual report Mr. Ellerington, the Chief Constable of St. Helens, says that the reason for a largo number a the fires up and down the connsry is over-insurance, which was more or less responsible for much incendiarism and certainly induced a careless- ness which was the cause of many tires. THE WHITE PLAGUE. ST. HELENS SANATORIUM SCHEME.

It was reported to the St. Helens Health Committee that the Sanatorium Sub-Committee had considered the advisability of formulating a scheme for the provision of s small-pox hospital in conjunction with the proposed new hospital for consumptives. It was resolved that the chairman and the medical officer be tuthorised to interview the Local Government Board to ascertain if the Board would be prepared to approve of such a scheme. The Chairman (Dr. Bates) said the reason of that resolution was that under the new Insurance Act there would be an advantage to those local authorities that were early in the field in making provision for the treatment of consumptives. At present they bad a smallpox hospital at Haydock. They were looking for a site for the new hospital for consumptives, and they might arrange a scheme that would be more beneficial to the town and less costly if they could have a portion of the site used for the second purpose. Both sets of buildings would be quite isolated, and in one corner of the site a building could be used for smallpox. They recognised that the Local Government Board might have some objection to such a scheme, and he suggested that the medical officer shonld interview Dr. Newsome, of the Local Government Board. div.head: TALKS ON HEALTH.
div.p: TALKS ON HEALTH.
[Br A FAMILY DOCTOR.]
OUR SHORT STORY.

I am going to tell you a story this week. It is not quite time for a sermon, but if I do not remind you this week of your duty to the religion of health, do not imagine that you are going to be let off the sermon altogether; wait till January and you will see. My story is entitled "The Doctor, the Shopman, and the Bicycle." The Doctor is the hero, the Shopman is the villain of the piece, and the bicycle is just thrown in as a make-weight. There is no heroine, and so there is no one for the hero to get married to and live happily ever after with on the last page. Once upon a time there lived a Shopman, who, not feeling well, decided to pay a visit to the Doctor. Entering the Doctor's room, he took a seat and said, "I am afraid there is something wrong with my system," and he described his symptoms in order that the physician might learn what was the matter and prescribe suitable remedies.
.—_--:o:----- N SOMETHING IN A BOTTLE.

The physician, having made his examina- tion and asked a few questions, declared thuswise. "You are disobeying many of the laws of health; you ought to have thirty-two teeth in your head, but you have none of your four wisdom teeth because you have no wisdom, eight of your teeth were so rotten they dropped out, nine of them are so decayed as to be useless, and the rest are embedded in diseased sockets from which oozes day and night a. poisonous discharge. I know that your workshop is small and stuffy and that the windows are not made to open, so that you never get any fresh air. You smoke packet after packet of cigarettes, which are as cheap and nasty as the picture given away with them is beautiful and in- structive. You are too generous in your sup- port of the liquor traffic, and, when on your way home, you Pass the Pig and Whistle, the Green Man, and the Cow and Coughdrop --well, pass them. "But am I not to have any medicine?" queried the Shopman. "No," replied our hero, "for if you will act upon my advice and alter your way of life you will get better very soon without a bottle of medicine." Whereupon the Shop- man grew very angry, and, thumping hi a fist on the table, shouted out that he came to the doctor for a bottle, not for a jawing. So the terrified doctor hied him forthwith to the bottle department and poured something out which could not do any harm, and gave it to the Shopman, who was very pleased and went away happy, hugging his bottle. A day or two after the Shopman came back, and said he did not think the medicine had done much good because he felt just as bad, but he would try another bottle.

div.head: DOCTOR'S BICYCLE.
div.p: THE DOCTOR'S BICYCLE.

The next day the Doctor found that he had a puncture in both the tyres of his bicycle (I knew you were waiting for the bicycle to come into the story), and being a wily person, and wag withal, he rode round to the Shopman, whose trade it was to mend and make bicycles, and said, "I am afraid I have something wrong with my system—my bicycle, I mean, for the road seemed very bumpy as I came along." "Yes," answered the Shopman, "you must let me take off the outer tyres, mend the punctures in the inner tyres, and then you will ride quite comfort- ably." "Oh, but would it not be better to put a little varnish on the mud-guard?" asked our hero: with an anxious face; "I would much rather you put a little varnish on than mend the punctures." But the Shop- man said he knew his business, and that the only thing to do was to mend the punctures. Whereupon the Doctor grew very angry, thumped his fist on the counter, and shouted out in a loud voice: "When I come to a bicycle shop, I come for a bit of varnish, not to have a puncture mended." Where- upon the terrified Shopman hied him forth- with into the shop to get the varnish, which he hastily put on the mudguard. Then the Doctor rode away with a satisfied smile on his bicycle (it was the Doctor who was smiling, not the bicycle), and aloug lie went, bumpety, bumpety, bump, to the astonishment of the passers-by.

div.head: HAPPY ENDING.
div.p: A HAPPY ENDING.

The next day the Doctor went round to the Shopman again and exclaimed: "I do not: think your varnish on the mudguard has clone much good, because I still noticed that funny: bumpy feeling as I rode along, but I will try another coat of varnish, and if that does not do I shall have to go to another Shopman." At this; the Shopman nearly burst into tears, as he did not want to lose a good customer, and thought the Doctor must be mad. So he spoke up and told the Doctor straight that he had been all his life mending -bicycles and that he knew his business, and if only the Doctor would trust him and follow his advice and let him put the bicycle in order in his own way he would do his best-, and would guarantee that the Doctor would be satis- fied. "Yes," answered the Doctor, "and I have been all my life mending human bodies, and I know my business, and if only you will trust me, I will do my best and will soon put you right." So the punctures were mended, the bumpy feeling disap- peared, and, what is more, the Shopman followed the good advice and lost his bumpy feeling inside. The two became fast friends, and when the Doctor married a beautiful young lady (aear me, I was afraid a heroine would creep in somehow!) the Shopman spent four shillings on confetti. ----:o:
WAX IN THE EAR.

Wax in the ear is not a disease; it is natural to have wax in the ears; it is only when it has accumulated into a large lump that it is necessary to have it removed. You must never under any circumstances what- ever poke pins and weird hooks and instru- ments down the ear. The drum is thin and sensitive and may easily be damaged, as I have seen many a time. If you are subject to the collection of wax in the ears you ought to have your ears syringed once in SIX or nine months. For a few nights before going to the doctor put some drops of warm oil into your . ear; this softens the wax and facilitates its removal. Only a man who 'ht.,o, trainal to ayntnino .ears eau say if

all the wax is out; after" one -iump has come out with the stream of water that is syringed into the ear, the ear-hole must be looked into with a mirror, using a bright light. Directly after syringing a small piece of wool must be put in the ear. If the wax has been in the ear for some time all ordinary sounds, such as the shutting of a door, the rumbling of traffic, and the voices of friends seem to be magnified, and you feel inclined to tell your friends not to shout at you. If you put wool in your ears be sure it is in one piece, not in two or three small bits, as one of them may get right into the ear and be left in perma- neatly, or until removed by a doctor. I have not infrequently withdrawn from the ear a piece of wool which was obstructing the hearing. Once I took out of one ear a piece of wool, a lump of wax, a strand of tobacco, and the broken end of a match. I told the patient that what he wanted was a dustman, not a doctor.

Does Efficiency Benefit the Workers? Sir,—The tone of Mr. Parker's last letter on the question of efficiency in production obviously denotes that nay last contribution on the subject was of such a vituperate character in Mr. Parlosr s estimation that he seriously considers this sufficient grounds for dis- continuing the discussion. If the language I used has hurt the feelings of Mr. Parker, or in any way proved me unworthy of corresponding publicly with Mr. Parker or anyone else or in any other journal, I am profoundly sorry. But for Mr. Parker to assert that I used invective because of lack of argument certainly proves that Mr. Parker either cannot, or will not perceive argument when it is there. Mr. Parker again asserts that the workers have got the benefit of efficiency in production and I again say that Mr. Parker has not given ma sufficient proof that be is right and lam wrong. Mr. Parker has again relied upon the statements that the workers have received the benefits of efficiency in prodncti n via competition. In spite of the fact that there occur in our newspapers reports of combinations of great industries, almost every week, and in spite of the fact that competition is practically dead in all our great industries, whether it be iron, wire, soap, leather, cotton, thread, mining of all descriptions, in ow rail- ways and canals, Mr. Parker will still keep on repeat- ing that competition brings down prices. Even admitting this argument to be true what does com- petition for work do for the workers ? Does not com- petition force the wages of the workers down to the lowest possible level of subsietence ? And must not the wages of the worker go lower as the price of commodities decreases, and se negative any advantage gained from decreased pt ices obtained thiough efficiency in production if any ? Mr. rattler says "let the readers go back thirty or forty years and compare the cost of the articles in daily use in which efficieney in production has had full scope and decide fur himself "&. " Begin at the child " he says " Look at the pictures, the crockery on the dresser. the cycles, and tramcars you ride in.' And then if you are not satisfied get Mr. Sauerbeck's index of figures showing you fleet the prices of commodities during the period intervening between the years 1870 and 1910 have been reduced to the extent of 22 per cent, and then if your joy loosens the purse centaining your savings due to efficiency in production go and discuss, you Mr. Workingman, with your wife, whether Switzerland or the Canary Islands will be the rendezvous of next year's peregrinations during your summer vacation. Of course, owing to efficiency in production your labour will be so lightened that you will now be able to have a decent holiday. If you will read Mr. Parker's letters and have a little imagination you will pull through alright. And if anyone tries to persuade you that the operation of production for profit does not allow a decent existence for the great mass of the workers proudly point to your jam made of saw-dust and saccharine, or your pictute frames and perambulators made under sweated labour conditions in spite of the fact that efficiency in production ought to have abolished sweating years ago. Bnt for goodness sake don't meotion the fact, that " Four or five can pro- duce the bread of a thousand. With the best machinery one workman can rroduce cotton cloth for 250 people, woollens for 300, or boots and shoes f 1,000, according to Mr. Atkinson an American statistical authority. And according to Ur. Seebohm Rowntree and Mr. Charles Booth there are 30 per cent, of people living in poverty. Mr. Rowntree s primary poverty line is 21s. Bd. The dietary allowed ' was more stringent than would be given to any able-bodied pauper in any Workhouse in England or Wales," and the wage should be expended as follows for a family of five :—Expenditure on food, 12s. 9d. ; rent and rates, 4s. ; clothing including boots, 23. 31. ; fuel, Is. 10l.; lighting, washing materiers, furniture, crcckery, 101.; total, 21s. Bd. According to Mr. Chiozza Money, Mr. Rowntree found that in York in a year of good trade 7,230 persons, representing 15', per cent, of the working cle,s, or 10 per cent, of the entire ;population 'of York, were living below a primary poverty line drawn at an income of 21s. 81. per week for a family of five paying only four shillings per week for rent. Mr. Rowntree also found 13,072 persons living in York under conditions which were but little above the primary line, making a total of 20,302 persons, or 28 per cent. of the population of York, Irving in want. Mr. Money's analyeis tells us that there are about 38,000,000 poor people in the British Isles, and Mr. Lloyd-George's latest outburst informs us that things are no better now than when Mr. Money wrote those words. And how does this affect Mr. Sauerbeck's figures about the reduction in the price of commodities? The only conclusion I can come to is that the people in 1870 were 22 per cent. worse off than they are now. To put it plainer the purchasing value in those days ;would be represented by about 18s. instead of 21s. Bd. According to Mr. Parker's own statmentsl the only increase the workers have received is a matter of about 9d. per week per head. I should like to ask Mr. Parker if he believes that 9d. aer head all round represents the sum total of the increased efficiercy in production during the past 40 years ? Think cf the great strides made in methcds of manufacture. We have our great steam- ships merely waiting the opnortunity of bringing to us all the good things nature provides for us. We have GO mile per hour locomotives waiting the opportunity of exchanging aed distributing manufactures. We have the great forces of electricity and steam harnessed to marvellous machinery which has multiplied a thousandfold our productive capaci y. And yet we shave thoueands of families whose only means of obtaluieg those perambulators, baby's bottles, crockery, dressers, which Mr. Parker so vividly paints for us, amounts to the fabulous sum of 10d. per week r family: These srallt benefit* aro infinitismal in comparison to the benefits the workers ought to have received if the real benefits accruing to the efficiency in production had been banded down to them. Given a small piece of land, and a few of the rudest imple- ments of productien and the training our forefathers bad, there is not a family in England but what could obtain a livelihood that sveuld be luxurious in com- parison with the average living of the average workers of to-day. M. Parker admits that machinery does cause over-production and my contention is that • seeing that capital is concentrating into fewer and fewer hands the consuming power of the rich must decrease. And with the development of more efficiency in production in all the countries where the methods of production are highly developed and with the entrance of such nations as Japan and China into the industrial international field and their adoption of European methods of production, I say this question of over-production must become more and more acute. The latest industrial crisis in America where the whole nation were practically at a standstill supports my contention. I am afraid I have encroached too much already but I must say a word or two about Mr. Parker's little dig at me about my always emphasising the Socialist position. I emphasize it because I think that Socialism is the most sensible and scientific scheme of social and industrial re-organisation that has ever been conceived. If Mr. Parker can show me any better I am willing to -accept it. But I am not going to be led off the track with false ideas of making the workers more efficient in production, which practically amounts to more sweating, or Insurance Acts of the .present type, and if my pen is of any value I am going to do my best in not allowing anyone else to be misled. I repeat again that so long as we have the land and implements of production, owned and con- trolled for the profit of a small class in the nation whatever developments there may be in science the workers' condition will be very little changed.— Yours truly,

Sir,—The Board of Trade Returns for the past 10 years, shows such a large increase that naturally many persons are somewhat jubilant over them. In some respects it must be acknowledge d that they have reason to be so, for the figures are most gratifying and on paper simply look splendid. But I venture to suggest that the principal and vital question to be considered in respect of these very large increases of trade is : Are those— i e., the workers and their employers—who have been engaged in producir g these increases, any better off as a result of their " toiling and their moiling ?" Well, the remarkable feature and irony d the whole transaction is, that after acc )mplishing this vast increase the workers are actually in a worse position than they were 10 years ago, owing to the fact that the extra increase in wages has been more than swallowed up in the increased cost of living, and also that in proportion to the increased output, properties have diminished, owing to increased cost of produc- tion, rates and taxes &c Such is the wonderful result, of our civilisation and legislation up to date, and the outlook at the moment is not reassuring. At the s .me time I am optimistic enough to think it is only a passing cloud. No one will, I think, venture to deny that the worker is entitled to the fruits of his labf ur and that he does not as a rule obtain more than an existirg wage. Whilst on the other hand the employer who in many cases works as hard as any of his employes, Ircs considerable difficulty in obtaining a due reward fir. his enterpri-e. There are those who, at the present juncture, are advising the workers to " strike " as a remedy for improving their condition. This advice is not only unsound but distinctly foolish and those who accept the advice are the most foolish of all fur they are invariably the greatest sufferers. No Labour problem has ever yet been settled by a strike and cannot in the nature of things be so settled. As capital and labour are part and parcel f each other they must work in harmony and agreement together and at the same time be assisted by judicious legislation— in order to achieve beneficial results. As the legisla- tion machinery is unfortunat,ly slow, employers and employees should in the meantime refer to and abide by the decision of Conciliation Boards. Humanity has never yet been able to devise a better way of settling a dispute other than that of arbitration.— Yours truly,
E. ENGLAND.

div.head: Mr. H. Smith, M.P., and Picketing.
div.p: Mr. H. Smith, M.P., and Picketing.

Sir,—ln your paper on Saturday, December 30th, 1911, I read with interest the correspondence (sent to you for publication) between Mr. H. Smith, M.P., and the Secretary of the A.W.S. re the Trades Disputes Act, 190 G. One feels tempted (even after the explanation given by Mr. Smith) to ask why it was that it took him from the beginning of October to nearly the end of December to answer the letter, if he is the friend of the Trade Unionists in Warrington and elsewhere that he wou'd have us believe ? How different his letter seems to the action he took in the House of Commons some time ago? Perhaps it would not be out of the way to quote one of the questions he put to the Prime Minister : Mr. Harold Smith asked the Prime Minister whether his attention had been called to the recommendation of the Railway Commission to the effect that members of the A.S.R.S. should not be permitted ta incite or coerce by threats or by any form of intimida- tion men who desire to give their labour, and if they proposed to introduce legislation to carry into eff.!ct the recommendation of the corc mission ? The Prime Minister said the passage referred to did not mention the A.S.R.S.,.nor did it recommend legislation. Let the Trade Unionists of Warrington take note. I think the question can not he too often asked Mr. Smith, why is it that he speaks of the Trade tinionists now as law- abiding citizens, when his procedure in the House of Commons and his letter to "Spectator" were anything but friendly. For the benefit of the Trades Unionists in Warrington I should like to suggest two reasons : First because Mr. Smith has come to realise that there is no hope of the act in question being repealed, secondly because the working men of Warrington are taking note of his doings and ha has been acquainted of the fact.

The old adage still applies. "Be sure your sins will find you out." So Mr. Smill.l tries to bridge the gulf by his letter. But the party which Mr. Smith belongs to is the party which has done all in its power to cripple the Trade Unionists. What party was it but the Tory party who cheered to the echo the action of the present government in the House of Commons during the strike last summer when the information was given about the military being sent out to help the employers against the workingmen. who were fighting for their existence ? If Mr. H. Smith is really a friend of the Trade Unionists let him leave the party which is the greatest enemy to them and then we shall believe he is in earnest. For the present I would suggest Mr. Smith is a friend of the monopolist class first and a friend of the Trades Unionists afterwards.—Youra
