div.head: COURT THEATRE.
div.p: COURT THEATRE.
WARRINGTON DRAMATIC SOCIETY.
"When We Were Twenty-One."

In many respects quite a notable success has been achieved by the old-established Wartington Dramatic Society this week. The annual performances for' well-known charities have been played to mowded houses instead of the small but select gatherings of recent years, and the company has acquitted itself in a fashion well worthy of the increased patronage. One wishes that tbe apparent change in public apprecia- tion were as real and permare,nt as the well-filled seats of the Royal Court lheatte suggested each even- ing ; but there were extraneous circumstaLces which contributed largely to the success of the p-oducti tn. Perhaps the Member for the Borough will (souse Us for incl.nl;ng him among the "extraneous circumstances," particularly as we now make amends by largely attributing the ebullition ef public interst to his having j Aned the Society as a player and producer. Mr. smith has a reputation for talent and proficiency in amateur theatricals which no one ventures to question, and his accession to the ranks of the Society is a welcome one and calculatsd to add greatly to its strength. Time was when the Society commanded public support in a much wider degree than has been the case of recent years. The falling-off has, happily, not beea due to a deterioration in the quality ci the performances, but to a change in the taste and habits of the people ehich one finds just as clearly reflected in the support given locally to classical concerts, and other entertainments of a superior character. We should like to think that the Dramatic Society was once in >re coming into its own, aticl reee'vieg that share of alit. r elation a-hick is undoubtedly its due. The dramatic venture which has occupied the Theatre stage during the first three nights of this week proves conclusively that then) is no scarcity of talent among even the youngest of the members. Mr. E. V. Esmond's comedy, "" When We Were Twenty-one "has given some of them an opportunity of winning their spurs which has been taken with hoth hands, but we feel that a play might have been chosen which would in all respects have c nsiderably transcended the one u.ader notice. In the first place it is too old-fashioned for present-day taste, too sentimental,and too bald in the opportunities it attends for dramatic talent. True, the lines of two or three principals are set in pleasant enough places, but with so small a cast there should be a mere equal division of both the labour and the "plums." Apart. from Richard Carew°, Phyllis, and "the Imp,' no one else has much to do beyond maintain a none-Lo- exacting character and move easily through the scenes. Briefly, the story which is unfolded tells of the stewardship for a dead friend's child which is under- taken by four contemporaries, Richard Careive, Sir Horace Plumely, Bart. (commonly called Waddles), Colonel Miles Graham (the Seldier man), and Terence McGrath (the Doctor). Till he is twenty-one "the Imp" does not appear to have 'done anything to justify so suggestive and uncouth a descrip- tion, but with manhood's advent he contracts a sudden alliance with _a "creature on the

walls " one Firefly, of music-hall fame. Consternation reigns in the breasts of Carew() and the trinity of "old boys." The reclamation of the youngster provides us with some fiery episodes and leads to a compound of love-affairs between" the Imp," Carewe,and Phyllis which develops on interest- ing and unsuspected lines. Phyllis is engaged to the transgressor—both have grown into the engagement —and both fall out of it with equal readiness. Then follows the mutual discovery of the tenderest senti- ment between Phyllis and Carevre, and the last act sees the awakening of the forty-year old man to the undreamt-of happiness. Mr. Smith was admirable as Carew e, the father-elect of young Richard. He was tender, admonitory, and self-sacrificing, and Pourtrayed an attractive character with manifest insight and skill. We liked him lost in the opening scene, when amid hallowed associations and joyous recollections, the four old friends " make a night of it." The spirit of camaraderie evident in all that Mr. Smith said or did reflected itself in the demeanour of that jolly trinity, Plumely, Graham, and McGrath. How they yarned, and drank, and played together. They were typical of " the good old English gentleman." Mr. Eidney Wellhead had one of those parts which display his talent for light comedy at its best —he was fat and fussy, simple and solicitous—a man with a joke for everyone and a character that inspired affectionate regard. Mr. G. R. Williamson was " the soldier man " to the life —spruce, corteous, and manly, while H. M. Ashton fulfilled very accurately the general conception of the merry medico with a touch of the brogue. All three men were individually interesting and it seemed a pity that they filled in so much of what was purely back- ground in the comedy. "The Imp" was capitally impersonated by Mr. Frank Richmond, who was very engaging in his early appearances in the role, and developed an altogether admirable display of anger and passion in the later passages with Carewe. Weakness or hesitancy would have ruined the part, but Mr. Richmond was tenderness or fire as the occasion demanded, and undoubtedly scored one of the individual successes of the performance. Miss Dorothy Browne had a charming, if exacting role, as Phyllis, and one cannot withhold a very warm appreciation of the great advance she has made as an actress since joining the society. There was naturalness, grace and charm in all she did, and her two great scenes with "the Imp" and Carew° were rendered remarkable by the talent she displayed for exhibiting raillery, emotion, and a captivating girlish innocence. Fu'l of artistic excellence, too, was the part played by Miss Gladys Adams as Mrs. Ericson. She would doubtless have been more at home in a lighter, brighter rae, and we hope to see her again when opportunity gives greater scope for the expression of natural gifts rather thau studied effect. The minor parts of Herbert Corrie and Dodd (a maid) were adequately played by Mr. Walter Young and Miss Bessie Forehaw. One scene —a room in Richard Carewe's flat—is all that the presentation of the comedy demands, but this scene was put on with an eye for realism and effect which speaks highly for Mr. Smith's attention to detail in the externals. -

_ Prior to the main performance there was a very amusing curtain-raiser "That Brute Simmons," a low- life comedy which suffered only from the want of condensation. Miss Bessie Forshaw displayed unfore- seen s as the voluble Mrs. Simmons, with an accent redolent of Limehouse, and fairly tiolc the honours of the Act. Mr. MoAey cleverly impersonated Bob Ford, sailor and donkey-man, but Mr. Geoffrey Dodd hardly succeeded in getting down t 3 the reqnisite level, and was not convincing as a British workingman. Mr. Arthur Browne (hon. treasurer) and Mr. J. W. Bullen (hon. secretary) were again responsible for the business arrangements, while the duties of stage- manager were in the efficient hands of Mr. C. H. Wood. The scenery was provided by Mr. A. M Loader, who, as usual, showed practical interest in the amateur production at his theatre.

div.head: BIG ATTRACTION NEXT WEEK. "THE QUAKER
div.p: BIG ATTRACTION NEXT WEEK. "THE QUAKER

On Monday next there will be a great attraction at the Royal Court Theatre, where "The Quaker Girl," from the Adelphi Theatre, London, will be in posses- sion. "The Quaker Girl" is one of the most success- ful musical plays that London has yet seen. This is the actual company from the Adelphi Theatre and they travel over GO persons and 10 tons of scenery and electrical properties. The first scene represents a country village and it is here that we first see the band of merry Quaker maidens, and get introduced to Tony, Prudence, Madam Blum, Captain Charteris, and that eccentric Quaker gentleman Jerry, who will persist in causing considerable merriment, to the great disgust of his Quaker papa, who gives him the cold shoulder and declines to be a party to such behaviour. The second scene shows Madam Blum's dressmaking salon in Paris and introduces in some special songs Miss Josset Ellis. who has played with success in " Our Miss Gibbs." The third scene represents the great ballroom scene in Paris and is said to be one of the most magnificent scenes ever placed on any stage. The dresses are the very latest creations of Paris and the stage is one blaze of colour. . .

Mr. Dance, the well-known Musical ccmedy magnate is sending his largest company, the many "stars," that will appear including Frank H Ctimp, J W Hoop.r,Charles Ross, Angus Strong, Powell Eastbury and that great comedian, John T MacCallum, and Mesdames Jossett Ellis, Dora Langham, who plays Prudence, and Olga Moira. The box office at the theatre is now open for advance booking and seats should be secured at once. UNDER TWO FLAGS." For the last three evenings of the week the management had secured a dramatic attraction of more than average interest in, the stage version of
NOME

Onida's famous novel "Under two flags." The play is full of the clash and colour of military life and there ;is also a powerful love element. Mr. J. C. Lodge-Percy's company is a highly capable one and the interest of the story is never allowed to flag. Mr Lodge-Percy gives a clever and convincing portrayal of the hero—the Hon. Bertie Cecil, afterwards Corporal Victor. He makes a manly, unflinching "soldier of FraLce" and invests every word and action with full meaning. The chief personal triumph falls to Miss Henrietta Schrier, as the irrepressible, vivacious and fearless Cigarette. She interprets every mood of an exacting part in a manner which never fails to go home to the audience, and from beginning to end she is prime favourite. The other parts are creditably sustained and the production is well mounted.

REV. W. COOPER REPLIES TO MR. HAROLD SMITH, M.P.

[TO THE EDITOR "WARRINGTON EXAMINER,"I Sir,—As Mr. Harold Smith has thought fit to publish the correspondence between him- self, and myself, I think I may legitimately claim for myself the right of a rejoinder, see- ing that I had not this privilege in time for the press after the issue of his letter of last week. This letter was only received by me on Friday evening: too late for a reply either to himself or to the press. For some reasons, I am rather glad that he has given the public the opportunity of reading the correspondence. Some of the language of Mr. Smith's letter of the sth inst., is unfortunately open to either a charitable or an odious interpretation. Perhaps he will not mind saying in clear and definite language, what view he takes of my conduct in this matter.

When I used the sentence complained of in my speech at the Thewlis-street schools, I had in mind certain facts of Tory Tyranny which have come under my personal observa- tion, and which subsequently have been fully corroborated, where people have been compelled to attend a Church against their conscience, in the fear and under the threat of being deprived of their employment or of being expelled from their homes, and having to seek employment in another part of the country:._. _ _ _

Now, Sir, Mr. Smith must understand that, as these things have not occurred in the constituency-which he represents, I consider he has no locus standi in this matter at all. Further, I definitely refuse, for the sake of the poor people who are subject to this tyrannical oppression, to publish any further particulars even in spite of Mr. Smith's challenge.

For s—ome reason or other, Mr. Smith seems to have a notion that he is the recognised censor of the Liberal platform. This, not- withstanding, so long as I am a burgess of Warrington, I shall claim for myself the privilege of openly and frankly criticising anything of a public nature which does not commend itself to my judgment. Yours, &c., WILLIAM COOPER.

WEIGHTS AND MEASURES INSPECTION

It will be of interest to shopkeepers to know what are the precise powers of •an in- spector of weights and measures who comes into the shop. Ilas he any right to walk in in the fashion that he does, and say, "I want to see your weights and scales and measures"? And the answer is that he has the right. If you have your doubts as to who he is, or anything of that kind, you may request him to produce his warrant; ,and he is bound to produce it. If he has not got his warrant with him, you are not bound to produce your weights and measures for his inspection. A heavy penalty awaits the persons who shall have the temerity to neglect or refuse to produce for inspection such things as the inspector calls for, lie may call for "all weights, measures, scales, balances, steel-yards, and weighing- machines in your possession or on your -ire- reises." The word "all" should be particu- larly noticed. You are to understand that theinspector cannot seize or forfeit any, weights, measures, etc., except such as arEr used for trade, or in your possession or custody for use for trade. But he has the right to call for and inspect all weights, measures, etc., in your possession or on your premises, whether they are there for use for trade or 'not. When you take your weights and measures to be tested by the local inspector, you have to pay certain fees to him. It is rather curious that although the local authority gets the benefit of these fees, the local authority has no power to abolislr them. There was a County Council not long ago which decided to discontinue charging. fees for the testing and verification of weights and measures. They thought they would pay the inspectors out of the general rate. This was by way of encouraging small tradesmen to come and have their weighte and measures tested frequently. But an un- sympathetic and legally minded auditor of the Local Government Board, who came down from London to audit accounts of that County Council .surcharged the County Council with the amount of fees that ought to have been received. An appeal to the High Court only resulted in the auditor's, acoount being confirmed; and it was de. cided, therefore, that the fees in question must be charged. No discount can be given; but just as the local authority must charge fees as specified by the Act of Parliament, so also it is the law that they must not charge more than the fees specified in the Act of Parliament.

Eighteen small holdings of from 30 to 50 acres each have been formed at Haslington and Oakhanger Moss, and numerous sets of farm build- ings for small holders are being erected, for which there is a considerable demand. The historic old Cheshire manion Haslington Hall, which was included in the purchase, is held in hand for the present.
